title: Unit of a write call
question: What is the unit a caller hands to MemSpine v2 and the unit stored as raw (L0) evidence: one message, a user/assistant turn pair, a caller batch, or a typed source envelope that covers messages and documents alike?
today: Several doors: write() for one record (engine.py:1672), write_messages()/write_episode() store one episodic record per message (engine.py:4270, 4368, 4578), ingest() chunks a document into resource records (engine.py:11778); each door has its own options and stamping.
others: Mem0 add() takes a string, dict or list and the caller decides whether one turn or a whole session is one call; Memori stores one wrapped exchange (user+assistant pair) per LLM call; Hindsight retain takes items with document_id and chunks them to 3,000 characters; Mnemon batch-creates 1 to 1,000 records per call.

options.label: Per-message records, separate doors (today)
options.detail: Keep write / write_messages / ingest as separate verbs; each message is one episodic record.
options.note: Finest provenance, but three doors stamp time, scope and trust in three ways.

options.label: Turn pair as the unit
options.detail: Store a user message and the assistant reply as one record.
options.note: Fewer rows, but who said what is blurred and multi-party chats do not fit.

options.label: Caller batch is the unit
options.detail: Whatever one call carries becomes one raw item and one extraction input.
options.note: Behaviour depends on how the caller batches; citations lose line precision.

options.label: Typed source envelope, per-message raw
options.detail: One intake contract: a source (conversation, document, tool log, asset) with ordered segments, each segment stored as its own L0 record; write_messages and ingest become thin adapters over it.
options.note: One place for stamping, idempotency and versioning; a refactor of the doors.

why: RV01 and RV07 need source ids, versions and lineage on every raw input; one envelope gives them once instead of per door, and per-message raw keeps line-level citation (RV02). Adapters keep the current API working.

title: What a write receipt guarantees
question: When a write call returns, what should the receipt promise: raw stored and searchable, raw stored only, everything derived, or raw stored plus a durable derivation intent the caller can poll?
today: The WRITE event is appended and every projector (SQL, LanceDB, Tantivy) applies it before return (engine.py:13479); window extraction runs later in a non-durable in-process queue (workers/windows.py:326) and the receipt says nothing about it.
others: Hindsight waits for extraction, embedding and storage by default (async=false); MemOS fast mode writes raw windows durably and enqueues fine extraction; Honcho commits messages and schedules deriver work as background tasks, so the 201 does not even mean queued; MemMachine returns after raw, index and semantic enqueue finish together.

options.label: Raw plus inline projections (today)
options.detail: Return after the event and all projections are applied; derivation status unknown.
options.note: Read-your-writes for raw turns, silent loss of derived work.

options.label: Raw durable only
options.detail: Return after the log append; projections and derivation follow asynchronously.
options.note: Fastest, but a read right after the write may miss the turn.

options.label: Fully synchronous
options.detail: Return only after extraction and every derived layer are committed.
options.note: Strong freshness at 13-49x the hot-path latency (RV10).

options.label: Raw searchable plus derivation intent
options.detail: Keep A, and also persist a derivation intent in the same transaction; the receipt carries its id and a status call reports pending / done / failed per layer.
options.note: Honest receipts; needs the durable queue (W-13).

why: RV01: raw turns surviving is not the same as derived work surviving; an intent written with the raw event is the cheapest way to make derivation recoverable and visible without paying the inline model call.

title: Idempotency key for retried writes
question: How should v2 recognise a retried or replayed write so the same message is never stored twice: content dedup only, an engine-derived fingerprint, a caller-supplied message id, or both with source versions?
today: No caller idempotency key exists (no idempotency_key field in the write API, engine.py:1672); write_messages embeds up front so a failed embedding raises before any turn is written (engine.py:4302), but a retry after a partial batch duplicates turns; episodic writes are plain WRITE events with no dedup (engine.py:4977).
others: EverMemOS dedupes buffered messages by message_id; Hindsight keys documents by document_id and skips unchanged chunks by hash (delta retain); Cognee dedupes raw data by content hash at add(); Mnemon stores every record raw with no dedup.

options.label: No key (today)
options.detail: Rely on caller discipline; semantic dedup catches some repeats later.
options.note: Retries after a crash duplicate raw turns and everything derived from them.

options.label: Engine fingerprint
options.detail: Key = hash(namespace, source id, segment index, content); a repeat is a no-op returning the existing record.
options.note: Works without caller help, but a genuine repeated message ('ok') in the same position needs the index to stay distinct.

options.label: Caller message id
options.detail: Accept an external id per message and dedupe on (namespace, source, id).
options.note: Exact when callers send ids; does nothing when they do not.

options.label: Caller id first, fingerprint fallback, versioned
options.detail: Use the caller id when present, else the B fingerprint; a same-id write with different content becomes a new source version, not a duplicate or a silent overwrite.
options.note: Covers retries and edits; ties into re-ingest (W-24).

why: RV01 asks for at-least-once execution with idempotent visible effects; that only holds end to end if the raw intake itself is idempotent, and versioning edits is what G-W46 needs later.

title: Times stamped on every raw input
question: Which clocks does v2 stamp on a raw input at intake: one valid_from plus recorded_at as today, or separate source time, ingestion time and (for derived items) an effective event interval with precision?
today: A message's timestamp, else the batch valid_from, else now becomes valid_from (engine.py:4478); naive datetimes are read in read.naive_timezone with one warning (engine.py:4506); same-time turns of a session are ticked by microseconds (engine.py:4534); recorded_at is the ingestion time.
others: EverMemOS splits cells on calendar-day change, so source date drives segmentation; Hindsight passes an event date to the extractor and turns coarse dates into full spans; LightMem requires a session time_stamp on each message; Mem0 stores only created/updated times.

options.label: valid_from + recorded_at (today)
options.detail: One event time per record, ingestion time separately.
options.note: Unknown source times silently become 'now'.

options.label: Three clocks, unknown stays unknown
options.detail: source_at (utterance time, nullable), recorded_at (ingestion), plus effective interval and precision on derived items; no fallback to now when the source gave no time.
options.note: Correct backfill and relative-date anchoring; readers must handle null source time.

options.label: B plus declared source time zone
options.detail: Every source declares its zone (or 'unknown'); relative phrases resolve against the cited utterance in that zone.
options.note: Removes the naive-time guess; one more field for callers.

options.label: Ingestion time only
options.detail: Ignore source times; every record is dated when written.
options.note: Breaks any backfilled history.

why: RV04: utterance, ingestion and event time must be separate and unknown dates must stay unknown; backfilled histories and multi-zone users are generic cases, and the naive-time warning shows the guess is already a known weak spot.

title: Speaker, addressee and subject tagging
question: How should v2 record who spoke, to whom, and about whom on each raw input: opt-in tags, first-class record fields from structured input, fields plus subject inferred at extraction, or per-observer fan-out?
today: Perspective tags spk:/addr: only when the perspective layer is on (engine.py:4434); participants tags under write.participants=session (config/schema.py:1725); role is source.role; speaker/subject in window facts are emitted but never read (G-W49 now field).
others: Honcho attributes each message to a peer and fans one extraction out to every observing peer; Mem0 tags each fact attributed_to user or assistant; Hindsight classifies facts world vs experience; Nemori passes the speaker name only as a transcript label.

options.label: Opt-in tags (today)
options.detail: spk/addr/participant tags when switched on; nothing otherwise.
options.note: Off by default, so most stores have no speaker axis.

options.label: Always-on structured fields
options.detail: spk(m) and addr(m) are record fields filled from the message's speaker/name/addressee or role; no inference.
options.note: Cheap and exact; subject still missing.

options.label: B plus extracted subject and asserter
options.detail: Raw records carry spk/addr; each extracted item carries asserter and subject (sub(m)) from the extraction call, validated against the cited line's speaker.
options.note: Separates 'Bram said Ilse moved' from 'Ilse said she moved'; needs field consumers (RV03).

options.label: Per-observer views
options.detail: Fan each extraction out into one collection per (observer, observed) pair.
options.note: Theory-of-mind views for multi-agent; heavy for single-user stores.

why: The notation already reserves spk/sub/ask axes; RV02 and RV03 show a quote can support a different person, so asserter and subject must be stored and consumed. D stays a later multi-agent template (G-W48).

title: Which roles and echoes enter memory
question: What is the default intake policy for system, tool and assistant messages and for recalled memory echoed back into the conversation?
today: All roles are stored; skip_message_roles is empty, skip_injected_recall and tag_assistant_claims are off (config/schema.py:1407, engine.py:4408-4442); when the echo guard is on, a MARKER event records what was dropped (engine.py:4417).
others: Memori drops system messages and excludes its own injected history; MemOS strips recalled-memory blocks before preference extraction; memU host adapters drop harness injections and thinking blocks; LightMem shows only user messages to the extractor by default.

options.label: Store everything, guards off (today)
options.detail: Every role deposited and fed to derivation unless the operator configures skips.
options.note: Recalled memory can be re-deposited as new evidence (G to D self-contamination).

options.label: Store all raw, role-aware derivation
options.detail: Raw keeps every role for audit; derivation treats assistant text as proposed, tool output as evidence with its own trust, system text as excluded; echo guard on by default.
options.note: Keeps the audit trail while stopping echo loops.

options.label: Drop system/tool and echoes at intake
options.detail: Never store them at all.
options.note: Simple, but tool results that carry facts are lost and there is no audit.

options.label: User-only derivation
options.detail: Only user text reaches extraction.
options.note: Misses facts the user confirms by assent to an assistant turn.

why: H21 and the N1 firewall claim both rest on not re-depositing recalled memory; generic agents need tool output as evidence, and assent rules (G-P2) need assistant turns visible as proposals rather than dropped.

title: Firewall placement on the derivation path
question: Where does the Memory Firewall screen content once extraction runs online: raw writes only, raw plus every derived item with parent trust caps, or also the extraction inputs (quarantined turns and injected instructions never reach the prompt)?
today: Raw writes pass _screen_write (engine.py:4670): redaction, instruction regex, embedding outlier, size and protected keys; derived records from extract_graph pass _screen_derived (engine.py:4655); the parent trust cap applies only under integrity.enabled (engine.py:4717); the window prompt includes a no_injection partial.
others: Hindsight Memory Defense is opt-in and regex-only for secrets; Honcho neutralises '<message' tags so content cannot forge batch boundaries; Mnemon defends only at read ('notes are data, never instructions'); Mem0, MIRIX and LightMem have no write-time check.

options.label: Raw screen, derived screen, cap opt-in (today)
options.detail: Both doors screened; trust inheritance off unless integrity is on.
options.note: A derived item can outrank its least-trusted parent by default.

options.label: Raw only
options.detail: Trust the extractor; derived items inherit nothing.
options.note: Laundering path: a poisoned turn becomes a clean-looking fact.

options.label: Three gates, cap always on
options.detail: Screen raw; exclude quarantined turns from extraction windows and mark all input blocks as data; screen every derived item and always apply tau_Delta <= min parent trust.
options.note: Closes the extraction laundering path that online calls widen.

options.label: C plus model adjudicator on flags
options.detail: A local classifier or decider reviews only flagged items before quarantine.
options.note: Fewer false holds at a model call per flag.

why: N1 (the paper's strongest claim) is a proved cross-agent reach bound; an online extraction call that sees quarantined turns or skips the parent cap would break it. The cap is already code (MTI-D), so the change is a default plus an input filter.

title: Provenance class and confirmation at write
question: How is the provenance class src(m) (user-stated, assistant-proposed, user-confirmed, tool) assigned at write, and what may promote an assistant proposal to a confirmed fact?
today: Trust comes from the role matrix (operator/system 0.9, user 0.7, assistant 0.5, tool 0.4, external channels 0.3; core/firewall.py:292); I48 src:inferred tagging and its trust cap are off (write.inferred, config/schema.py:1725); window facts carry no source field (G-P2).
others: MemOS keeps assistant content only if the user acknowledged it; Honcho has an assent-transfer rule in its deriver prompt; Cognee rejects assistant-only claims; EverMemOS gates by speech act.

options.label: Role trust only (today)
options.detail: No provenance class on derived items; inference tag opt-in.
options.note: An assistant suggestion can become a user 'fact' through extraction.

options.label: Class from extraction source field
options.detail: Each item carries source user_stated / assistant_proposed / user_confirmed / tool, mapped to src(m); assistant_proposed trust capped.
options.note: Relies on the model labelling assent correctly.

options.label: B plus checked assent
options.detail: user_confirmed only when a cited user line shows assent (not mere acknowledgement such as 'ok, thanks') and the span binds the proposal; otherwise downgraded to assistant_proposed.
options.note: Code check guards against sycophantic promotion.

options.label: Drop assistant-only claims
options.detail: Never derive from assistant text without a user line.
options.note: Safe but loses agent self-knowledge (what it did or recommended).

why: G-P2 and the G-W49 prompt v2 (assent vs acknowledgement) put the field in the schema; RV02 says entailment needs a code check, and the record state G1 already defines src(m), so this fills an existing slot.

title: Routing writes to memory types
question: Who decides which memory type a write lands in: the caller per call, a rule router, an LLM router, or a fixed rule that raw always lands in episodic/resource and typed layers only arise through derivation or an explicit keyed write?
today: write() defaults to semantic (engine.py:1672) and the caller picks memory_type; write_messages always writes episodic, ingest writes resource; semantic writes take the dedup and conflict pipeline, others a plain WRITE (engine.py:4965-4993).
others: MIRIX runs a meta-manager LLM call that picks memory types per batch; MemOS lets the extractor label UserMemory vs LongTermMemory; MemMachine routes by target_memories; Hindsight routes everything through one retain path into world/experience facts.

options.label: Caller chooses (today)
options.detail: memory_type argument with a semantic default.
options.note: An unkeyed free-text write lands in semantic and skips raw provenance.

options.label: Rule router
options.detail: Rules on role, channel and shape (keyed fact, skill, plan) choose the type.
options.note: Predictable, but rules drift into content guessing.

options.label: LLM router
options.detail: A model call per batch chooses the types.
options.note: Flexible and expensive; adds a failure point on the hot path.

options.label: Raw first, typed by derivation
options.detail: Unkeyed content always lands as episodic or resource raw; semantic, procedural, prospective and others come from derivation (with parents) or from explicit keyed writes (entity/attribute, skill, plan).
options.note: Every typed record has lineage; the caller's explicit typed writes still work.

why: Lineage (G1 parent sets) and erasure cascades work only when typed records have raw parents; D keeps the explicit-key door (M13.3) while removing the parentless free-text semantic default.

title: Event log to projection hand-off
question: How do appended events reach the SQL, vector, lexical and graph projections in v2: inline before return, through a transactional outbox applied by workers, or a split where hot stores apply inline and heavy ones through the outbox?
today: _append_and_project appends the event, then applies every projector inline and checkpoints offsets (per call in a projection batch); catch_up replays the tail after a crash (engine.py:13479, 13576).
others: Mnemon rewrites its collection under a lock with fsync and atomic rename (no queue); EverMemOS writes markdown first and LanceDB lags by up to 10-15 s under load; MemMachine gathers raw, index and enqueue concurrently; Honcho schedules embeddings as background tasks after the response.

options.label: All projections inline (today)
options.detail: Every store updated before the call returns; offsets replayed on restart.
options.note: Simple and fresh; an online graph projector would slow every write.

options.label: Transactional outbox for all
options.detail: Event and projection intents committed together; workers apply projections.
options.note: Write latency flat, but raw turns are not searchable at return.

options.label: Split: hot inline, heavy via outbox
options.detail: SQL and lexical (and vector when the embedding is cached) inline; graph and derived projections through the outbox with idempotent apply and tombstone checks.
options.note: Keeps read-your-writes for raw while online derivation scales.

options.label: External stream
options.detail: Events go to a broker (Kafka / Redis streams) and projectors consume.
options.note: Multi-instance scale; heavy for a local-first engine.

why: RV06 and RV07 require transactional outbox and projection recovery for the online graph writer, while the current inline path is what makes raw turns searchable immediately; splitting keeps both.

title: Segmentation of turns for extraction
question: What unit of turns does each extraction call cover and what closes it: the adaptive window, a token-gated batch, an LLM boundary call, one turn with context, or the adaptive window plus time-gap rules?
today: Adaptive window per namespace and session: closes at topic shift (cosine below the store's running mean - 2 sd after 20 learned pairs), 6 turns, 1,500 tokens, 120 s idle, session end or flush (core/window.py:1-80, write.window_* in config/schema.py:1757-1777); window_max_turns 1 gives per-turn mode.
others: Honcho batches 512-1,024 tokens per observed peer; LightMem flushes a 512-token buffer with optional embedding/attention topic cuts; Nemori and EverMemOS ask an LLM for boundaries (EverMemOS splits on calendar-day change and 4 h gaps); Hindsight cuts 3,000-character chunks at turn boundaries.

options.label: Adaptive window (today)
options.detail: Topic, turn, token, idle and session boundaries; no model call.
options.note: Small windows (mean about 186 tokens) give good citations; time gaps inside a session do not cut.

options.label: Token-gated batch
options.detail: Accumulate until N tokens or max age, then one call.
options.note: Fewer calls, but batches mix topics.

options.label: LLM boundary call
options.detail: A model decides where episodes split.
options.note: Best boundaries in principle, one more call per batch.

options.label: Per turn with context lines
options.detail: One call per new turn, previous turns shown as CONTEXT only.
options.note: Freshest edges; about 5x the calls of 6-turn windows.

options.label: Adaptive window plus time-gap rule
options.detail: A, plus a cut when the source-time gap between turns exceeds a gap learned per store (or a calendar-day change), and per-turn mode kept as a setting.
options.note: Cheap generic fix for long silences inside one session id.

why: ADR-066 chose the adaptive window for zero-call segmentation; a time-gap boundary is the one cue the survey shows others use that it ignores (W-04 gives the source time). Per-turn mode stays a setting for freshness-critical agents (G-W49).

title: Online extraction: async, inline or deferred
question: When does the online extraction call (G-W49) run relative to the write: asynchronously right after the receipt, inline before return, deferred to a sleep batch, or async with an optional read barrier that waits for pending windows?
today: window_async true: window calls run in a background task after write returns, idle-debounced; false runs them only at flush_windows, close_session or sleep (config/schema.py:1774); edges then wait in an in-memory buffer for the sleep stage extract_graph (workers/windows.py:808).
others: Graphiti add_episode extracts inline (2 calls plus dedupe calls per new fact); Hindsight retains synchronously by default; Mnemon and memU make zero model calls on write and fold in background jobs; MemOS returns after raw write and enqueues fine extraction.

options.label: Async after receipt, edges at sleep (today)
options.detail: Facts land shortly after the write; graph edges only after sleep.
options.note: Graph is stale until sleep runs.

options.label: Inline before return
options.detail: Write waits for the extraction call and deposit.
options.note: Always fresh; 13-49x hot-path latency (RV10).

options.label: Deferred batch only
options.detail: Extraction runs only in sleep or scheduled jobs.
options.note: Cheapest; facts and edges absent between jobs.

options.label: Async online deposit plus read barrier
options.detail: Facts and graph items deposit right after the write through the shared emit; a read may pass wait_for_pending (bounded timeout) to see the namespace's pending windows first; LLM merges stay at sleep.
options.note: Fresh graph without a slower write; callers who need read-your-derivations ask for it.

why: G-W49 measured a 9B call at about 2.7 s vs 55-210 ms hot path, so inline is ruled out by default; agents that act on the next turn need a way to wait, which a barrier gives without slowing every write. Gate: p95 turn-to-searchable-edge and queue delay (G-W49, RV10).

title: Durable derivation queue and acknowledgement
question: How is pending derivation work persisted so a crash or stop never loses it: the in-process deque as today, window state markers in the event log, a leased outbox with attempts and idempotent effects, or an external runner?
today: Window jobs live in a per-namespace deque (workers/windows.py:326) and are abandoned and counted on stop (workers/windows.py:568); take_edges clears pending edges before downstream acknowledgement and overflow drops the oldest batches (RV01, workers/windows.py:808-812); dbos and taskiq runners exist for sleep stages only (config/schema.py:265).
others: memU stages the cursor and promotes it only on commit; MIRIX claims triggers exactly once through a persisted cursor; Honcho shares a retry budget across instances and keeps errored items 30 days; Hindsight claims Postgres rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; Nemori and MemOS can lose derived work on some failure paths (RV19).

options.label: In-process deque (today)
options.detail: Fast and simple; lost on stop or crash.
options.note: Silent gaps in derived layers after any restart.

options.label: Window state as log markers
options.detail: window_opened / window_done / window_failed events; catch_up re-queues unfinished windows; cursor advances after deposit commit.
options.note: Small change (G-W27); no leases for multiple workers.

options.label: Leased outbox, at-least-once, idempotent effects
options.detail: Persist membership, source versions, attempts, leases and result state; deposit idempotently, then acknowledge; caps on backlog age and size.
options.note: Correct under multi-worker and crash; needs versioned keys (W-20).

options.label: External durable runner
options.detail: Run window jobs on the existing dbos or taskiq runner.
options.note: Durability from infrastructure; extra dependency for local use.

why: RV01 confirmed process-local jobs and pre-ack edge clearing; its gate is faults injected after inference and after partial deposit. B is the first step of C (same events), and C stays local-first inside SQL; D remains an adapter.

title: Malformed output, retries and dead letters
question: When an extraction reply is malformed, partly invalid, truncated or empty, what does v2 do: drop the section, validate per item with one diagnostic repair, persist failure reasons with retry eligibility and a dead-letter list, or split and retry halves?
today: Code-side JSON repair, per-section validation that fails closed (workers/windows.py:199, 236), auto-split into facts+edges / episode after 25% of the last 8 joint calls fail (workers/windows.py:375, 618-698); failed windows counted in jobs_failed; no repair re-ask (G-P4).
others: Hindsight auto-splits on output overflow, re-asks with a shape repair and retries async tasks up to 3 times; Mnemon re-asks once then halves the batch with two attempts each; Honcho marks terminal errors and keeps them 30 days; LightMem swallows exceptions with no retry.

options.label: Section fails closed (today)
options.detail: A bad section is dropped and counted; the rest lands.
options.note: One bad item in a unified list would drop the whole list (RV11).

options.label: Per-item validation plus one repair
options.detail: Keep valid items, re-ask once for the invalid ones with validator errors, forbid new items.
options.note: Recovers items at one bounded extra call.

options.label: B plus persisted failure state
options.detail: Record failure class (raised, malformed, valid-empty, truncated, size skip, partial commit), attempts and retry eligibility; truncation schedules the remaining lines instead of discarding them; dead-letter list kept for review.
options.note: Coverage loss becomes visible and recoverable.

options.label: Halving split retry
options.detail: On repeated failure split the window in halves and retry each.
options.note: Good for long batches; windows are already small.

why: RV11 (per-item validation, bounded attempts, no silent truncation) and RV19 (classify failure modes, a valid empty reply is not a failure) both point here; G-P4 gate is sections_dropped down with no new ungrounded items.

title: Schema of an extracted item
question: What does one extracted item look like: separate facts and edges sections as today, the G-W49 unified item list, a versioned assertion envelope that compiles optional graph edges in code, or free-text facts only?
today: Window call returns facts (atomic, dated, span-grounded), edges (src, rel, dst, fact) and an episode as separate sections (workers/windows.py:1-20, prompts/models.py); in facts_graph a relation can be emitted twice and speaker/subject/confidence are never read (G-W49).
others: Graphiti extracts nodes and edges in separate calls on add_episode (combined on bulk); Hindsight and Cognee take entities and relations from the same call; Mem0 extracts free-text facts with no edges; Memori stores (subject, predicate, object) triples with counts.

options.label: Separate facts and edges (today)
options.detail: Two sections, two validators, two deposit paths.
options.note: Duplicate relations and unread fields.

options.label: Unified item list (G-W49 v2)
options.detail: {s, r, o, text, kind state|event|fact, mode, neg, when, until, lines, span}; s/o nullable with literal values.
options.note: One list, fewer tokens; still triple-shaped.

options.label: Versioned assertion envelope
options.detail: B as v1 of a versioned envelope: text plus typed value, evidence spans, asserter and subject, modality and polarity, source time and event interval with precision, kind and occurrence, optional graph projection compiled in code; n-ary and list facts kept without fake entity nodes; every field has a named consumer.
options.note: One contract for facts and graph; unknown enum values fail closed per item.

options.label: Free-text facts only
options.detail: No structure beyond text and date; graph derived later.
options.note: Simplest; no online graph, no supersede seeds.

why: RV03: the schema needs consumers, literal and n-ary facts must not become fake nodes, and mode/neg/until need storage and read paths; the review's G-W49 contract lists exactly these field groups. B ships as envelope v1.

title: What the extraction call is shown
question: Which input blocks does the extraction prompt carry besides the NEW lines: nothing, CONTEXT lines plus KNOWN names, also the top existing facts under integer aliases with a replaces field, or a predict-calibrate step?
today: The window call sees only its own turns: no earlier facts, no adjacent windows (workers/windows.py; G-W4 not built); turns are cited as [n] and an out-of-range citation is dropped as facts_uncited (G-W36).
others: Mem0 shows the top 10 existing memories renumbered 0-9 and the last 10 messages; MIRIX shows each sub-agent its own rows with ids; MemMachine passes up to 50 profile features; Nemori predicts the episode from known facts and keeps only the gap; Graphiti shows previous episodes as context.

options.label: NEW lines only (today)
options.detail: Window turns, nothing else.
options.note: Coreference across windows fails; updates handled only by the ladder.

options.label: NEW + CONTEXT + KNOWN names
options.detail: A few previous lines as context (never extracted from) and a line of known entity names for the window's subjects.
options.note: Fixes pronouns and name drift at modest token cost; KNOWN suggests identity, never overrides evidence.

options.label: B + known facts under aliases
options.detail: Top-k live facts for the window's subjects as integer aliases with a replaces field that seeds the conflict ladder; reject unseen aliases.
options.note: Explicit supersede and fewer restatements; retrieval at write and cache identity changes (RV07).

options.label: Predict-calibrate
options.detail: Predict the window from known facts, extract only what was not predicted.
options.note: Fewer duplicate writes at two calls; may miss restated changes.

why: B is the G-W49 prompt v2 shape accepted after the Codex review; C (G-W4) is wave B and must prove itself on knowledge-update slices without loss (its gate), so it follows as an advanced step once B and W-20 identity land.

title: How extracted items are grounded
question: What check must an extracted item pass to be deposited: a normalised substring span as today, spans per assertion and per endpoint with rule checks on numbers, polarity and entity binding, plus selective semantic adjudication, or a model verifier on every item?
today: Facts pass a normalised substring check against the cited lines (workers/windows.py:148, 221); edges only need valid line indices (workers/windows.py:236); a matching quote may support another person, polarity or relation (RV02).
others: MemOS runs a grounding validator that marks assistant-only and user-denied content; Hindsight rejects degenerate facts; Honcho, Mnemon and LightMem require cited lines; Graphiti trusts the model and dedupes afterwards.

options.label: Substring span (today)
options.detail: Span must appear in a cited line.
options.note: Cheap; does not prove the item says what the span says.

options.label: Spans plus rule checks
options.detail: Span per assertion and per endpoint; numbers, units, qualifiers, negation and the bound names must appear in the cited evidence; failing items kept as uncertain, not promoted.
options.note: Deterministic, multilingual-safe if rules are script-neutral.

options.label: B plus selective adjudication
options.detail: Ambiguous bindings only (for example two people named in one line) go to a small local entailment model or the decider.
options.note: Spends model time only where rules cannot decide.

options.label: Model verifier on every item
options.detail: A second call checks each item against its evidence.
options.note: Doubles write cost.

why: RV02 confirms citations do not prove entailment and asks for per-endpoint spans, numeric/polarity checks and selective semantic adjudication; G-W49 gate needs grounding >= 95% measured on labelled cross-domain sets.

title: Extraction prompt rules and versioning
question: Which rule set and prompt style does the write extraction prompt use: v1 rules, the example-free v2 block, v2 plus shared partials for language and coarse dates with soft length guidance, or a long few-shot prompt?
today: window_extract prompt v1 (958 tokens in facts_graph mode) with a no_injection partial only; no same-language rule (G-P1), no length bound (G-P3), coarse dates parsed as day one (workers/pipelines.py:2912; G-P6); gold-lint skips _partials (G-P5).
others: Mem0 ships an 8.5k-token few-shot system prompt; Hindsight has same-language and full-span date rules; Honcho, Mnemon and LightMem use static example-free prompts; EverMemOS places a language module at head and tail.

options.label: Prompt v1 (today)
options.detail: Current rules and size.
options.note: Known gaps on language, dates, plans and denials.

options.label: Prompt v2, example-free
options.detail: About 353 tokens: CONTEXT and KNOWN as data, keep list members, mark plans/wishes/doubt, assent vs acknowledgement, nullable literals.
options.note: Shorter and more precise; token count still unverified (RV10).

options.label: v2 plus shared partials, soft caps
options.detail: B plus same_language.j2 (never translate names; keys stay English) and coarse-date-as-span in every write prompt; length as a soft validator warning, not a hard rule; prompt hash and version on every derived item; gold-lint covers partials.
options.note: Generic across languages and data; each rule screened separately.

options.label: Long few-shot prompt
options.detail: Many worked examples per rule.
options.note: Examples leak into outputs and cost tokens per call.

why: Codex accepted v2 (2df543d); RV15 warns hard 40-word caps erase lists and that language/date rules are not quality-neutral, so each ships behind its own screen; prompt hash on items is needed for cache identity (RV07) and cost manifests (RV10).

title: Entity resolution on the write path
question: How are names in an online extraction resolved to entities: only at sleep as today, in code online with new names marked pending for sleep reconciliation, with an online LLM dedupe per new entity, or by deterministic name ids only?
today: The EntityResolver (memories/associative/resolution.py:164) runs only in the sleep extract_graph sweep (resolve off | rules | llm): exact, alias table, top-15 by cosine, entropy gate, MinHash Jaccard >= 0.9, then optional LLM.
others: Graphiti resolves by exact name, entropy gate and MinHash before any LLM, then one LLM call for unresolved nodes; Hindsight uses pg_trgm candidates and a word compatibility check, no LLM; Cognee and Memori key entities by normalised name; Honcho trusts client peer names.

options.label: Sleep only (today)
options.detail: Online items carry raw names until the next sleep.
options.note: Graph fragments until sleep; reads see duplicates.

options.label: Online code resolution, pending merges
options.detail: Same ladder with llm=None, vectors cached per namespace and bounded; uncertain new names stored as pending_merge for sleep LLM reconciliation; homonyms kept apart by type and context.
options.note: Fresh graph with no extra call; thresholds need their own calibration (RV17).

options.label: Online LLM dedupe
options.detail: One model call per unresolved new entity.
options.note: Best online merges at many calls on new-entity-heavy text.

options.label: Deterministic name ids
options.detail: Entity id = normalised name; no fuzzy merging.
options.note: Merges homonyms and splits aliases.

why: G-W49 design resolves names in code and leaves LLM merges to sleep (ADR-066 call 3); RV17 requires MinHash and cosine thresholds be calibrated separately on held-out alias/homonym pairs and ambiguous entities preserved.

title: Identity key of a graph assertion
question: What makes two graph assertions the same record: (ns, src, rel, dst) as today, that key plus kind and an event occurrence id with archived keys sent to the ladder, a versioned assertion id separate from event occurrence with re-mentions corroborating, or a uuid per occurrence with a dedupe call?
today: _edge_key (workers/pipelines.py:1882) fingerprints (ns, src, rel, dst) without kind; the dated variant adds the day and numerals, so same-day repeats collapse and undated events have no occurrence; an archived state key short-circuits before the conflict ladder, so A then B then A is skipped (G-W50, RV05).
others: Graphiti keeps each edge occurrence with its own uuid and episode list and judges duplicates per fact with date and number qualifiers; Memori increments num_times on a repeated triple; Cognee checks edges against storage by identity.

options.label: Triple key (today)
options.detail: Same triple in a namespace is one record.
options.note: Collisions become frequent once deposits are online.

options.label: Kind + occurrence, archived to ladder (G-W50)
options.detail: Key = (ns, src, rel, dst, kind) plus cited turn ids for events; archived or superseded keys go through the ladder.
options.note: Small fix; a re-mention of one event in two windows becomes two events.

options.label: Versioned assertion id plus event resolution
options.detail: B, with a key version and old-key aliases; assertion identity, event occurrence and semantic dedup kept separate: a re-mention attaches as support to an existing occurrence when date and qualifiers match, otherwise opens a new one.
options.note: Correct counts and state returns; needs a migration.

options.label: UUID per occurrence plus LLM dedupe
options.detail: Every extracted edge is new; a model call decides duplicates.
options.note: Flexible, costs a call per new fact.

why: RV05 confirms the defects and asks for versioned keys separating assertion identity, occurrence and dedup, with migration; G-W50 (B) is its first step and the G-W49 prerequisite. Gate: A-B-A returns to A, two same-day events stay two, reruns idempotent.

title: Who chooses the integration operator
question: How is the integration operator (append, supersede, merge, coexist, contest) chosen for a new item: the deterministic ladder alone, the ladder seeded by extraction hints (kind, replaces alias, cardinality), an LLM ADD/UPDATE/DELETE decision, or deferral of all non-trivial cases to K_C?
today: A deterministic 13-rung conflict ladder (core/policies/conflict.py) returns NOOP / ADD / UPDATE / INVALIDATE / CONTEST with the rung named; 7 rungs on by default; cardinality is operator-declared per relation (workers/pipelines.py:2015, memories/semantic/write_pipeline.py:141); contest, merge_containment and perspective_key are opt-in.
others: Mem0 extraction is ADD-only; MemMachine and Honcho let an LLM issue DELETE then ADD and keep no history; Hindsight keeps raw facts append-only and reconciles at the observation layer per batch of 8; LightMem and MemOS merge or delete offline by LLM.

options.label: Rule ladder alone (today)
options.detail: Ladder decides from key, trust, time and tags.
options.note: Auditable; blind to what the text says changed.

options.label: Ladder seeded by extraction hints
options.detail: kind (state/event), a replaces alias and a 'changed from A to B' transition seed the ladder; the ladder still decides and names the rung; supersede only when the relation's cardinality is one.
options.note: Model proposes, code disposes; hints need W-16 C.

options.label: LLM decides the operation
options.detail: A model returns ADD / UPDATE / DELETE over neighbours.
options.note: Flexible; destroys history and lets text decide trust.

options.label: Append now, decide in K_C
options.detail: Online deposit only appends; supersede, merge and contest happen at consolidation.
options.note: Cheap online path; stale states visible until sleep.

why: BD-4 keeps supersede and contest with history; the ladder is the deterministic N1 guard (trust gate R1) and must stay the decider, while G-W4 and G-W49 show the extractor can supply the missing signal. The notation allows supersede/merge/contest to be deferred to K_C, so D remains the fallback when hints are absent.

title: Default when cardinality is undeclared
question: When a new value lands on an existing key whose relation has no declared cardinality and neither trust nor time decides, should v2 supersede (latest wins), coexist, contest (keep both, marked disputed), or coexist unless the item is a state with cardinality one?
today: Same-key writes go down the ladder, where a newer statement supersedes by default; coexist happens only for declared many relations or under perspective_key; contest_ties and contest_lower_trust are off (core/policies/conflict.py:60-90).
others: Nemori, EverMemOS and Mem0 keep both values (append-only, contradictions coexist); Mnemon appends a new dated value under the same state key; MemMachine and MIRIX overwrite; Cognee adds a non-destructive 'contradicts' edge when its detector is on.

options.label: Supersede latest (today)
options.detail: Newer same-key value retires the old one as history.
options.note: A second pet or employer silently retires the first.

options.label: Coexist always
options.detail: Both stay live; the reader resolves.
options.note: No lost values, stale states keep answering.

options.label: Contest when undecided
options.detail: Keep both, tagged disputed, until trust, time or the user settles it.
options.note: Honest; readers must present disputes.

options.label: Kind-aware default
options.detail: Events and facts coexist; states supersede only when the relation is declared or learned to be one-valued, otherwise contest; cardinality learned per relation from observed co-live values and reviewable.
options.note: Generic across domains without an operator listing every relation.

why: The G0 operator split makes cardinality a schema property; G-W49 limits supersede to cardinality one, and declaring every relation by hand does not scale to arbitrary workloads. Contest for undecided states keeps the H9 audit trail.

title: Images and attachments at ingest
question: How should attachments be handled at write: register identity only as today, describe them with an opt-in local vision model at ingest with asset hash and provenance, describe them on demand at read, or run a full document/vision parsing pipeline?
today: ingest.assets off by default; when on, each attachment's identity is registered and the record tagged asset:<id> with nothing downloaded at ingest (config/schema.py:1780, engine.py:4464); asset_vision none; vision model installed but not to be used (BD-8 user decision).
others: Hindsight accepts inline attachments with an image budget per chunk; Mem0 makes one vision call per image when enable_vision is on; EverMemOS has a parser module; MemOS has vision extraction; Nemori re-compresses images for size only.

options.label: Identity only (today)
options.detail: Asset registered, tagged, never described.
options.note: Visual evidence is invisible to every layer.

options.label: Opt-in description at ingest
options.detail: A local vision model writes a caption as a derived resource record with the asset hash, model and prompt as provenance; off by default.
options.note: Searchable visual facts; vision errors become memory.

options.label: On demand at read
options.detail: Describe an asset only when a read needs unresolved visual evidence.
options.note: Pays only when used; no recall through visual content.

options.label: Full parsing pipeline
options.detail: Document, table and image parsers at ingest for every source.
options.note: Broad coverage, heavy dependencies.

why: RV13 routes unresolved visual evidence to an opt-in extraction path with stored asset hash; B keeps the BD-8 hold (default off until the owner enables it) while defining the v2 contract, and C can reuse the same port.

title: Re-ingesting an edited document
question: When a stored document changes, does v2 re-ingest it whole, diff at chunk level and re-extract only changed regions, treat each version as a source version with derived items re-pointed or retired, or use content-defined chunking for stable boundaries?
today: Resource ingest is idempotent per (path, fingerprint) but re-ingests a changed document whole (memories/resource/store.py:54; G-W46).
others: Cognee diffs a document against stored chunks, re-extracts only changed regions and verifies the reassembly; Hindsight delta retain skips unchanged chunks by hash; memU re-embeds only changed lines; Cognee incremental_loading skips processed data.

options.label: Whole re-ingest (today)
options.detail: New fingerprint means a full new ingest.
options.note: Old derived facts linger beside new ones.

options.label: Chunk diff with parent reuse
options.detail: Unchanged chunks keep their records and derivations; changed chunks re-extracted; removed chunks tombstoned with their dependents.
options.note: Shifted boundaries can make most chunks look changed.

options.label: B on source versions
options.detail: Each edit is a new source version event; derived items record the version they came from and are retired or re-pointed when it is superseded; as-of reads see old versions.
options.note: Uniform with message edits (W-03) and erasure lineage.

options.label: C plus content-defined chunks
options.detail: Rolling-hash chunk boundaries so a local edit changes only nearby chunks.
options.note: Best reuse; chunk sizes vary.

why: RV07 asks for source ids and versions on all derived layers with tombstones against stale publication; versioned sources make document edits and message edits one mechanism. Not in the evaluation scope, so later (G-W46 wave D).

title: Backpressure when derivation falls behind
question: When writes arrive faster than extraction can run, what does v2 do: drop the oldest pending batches as today, coalesce windows without dropping evidence and mark sources underived for catch-up, reject writes, or shed derivation by priority?
today: write_messages batches embeddings and projection commits per call (engine.py:4302-4330); pending edge batches above WINDOW_PENDING_EDGES_MAX (5,000) drop the oldest and count edge_batches_dropped (workers/windows.py:810-812, config/constants.py:511); queue length and age are not capped.
others: Honcho gates on 512 pending tokens or 1,800 s age and caps input at 25,000 tokens; Memori's 512-slot queue rejects jobs when full; Mnemon caps 16 batches per background job; memU caps 10 sessions per run and re-offers the rest.

options.label: Drop oldest (today)
options.detail: Bounded memory, silent evidence loss.
options.note: Loss is counted but never recovered.

options.label: Coalesce and mark underived
options.detail: Adjacent pending windows of a session merge up to the token cap; beyond age or size caps, sources are marked underived and picked up by catch-up or sleep; nothing is dropped.
options.note: Freshness degrades, coverage does not.

options.label: Reject writes when full
options.detail: Return a retryable error (429) to the caller.
options.note: Pushes the problem to callers; raw intake should never fail for derivation reasons.

options.label: Priority shedding
options.detail: Under load skip low-priority sections (episode, edges) and keep facts; skipped work queued for sleep.
options.note: Keeps the most-used layer fresh; layers drift apart.

why: RV01: cap backlog age and size and coalesce without dropping evidence; with the durable queue (W-13) an underived marker is just a state, and the review lists queue age and write amplification as metrics to report.

title: Write-side cost ledger and budget
question: How much write-side cost accounting does v2 keep: call-1 counters as today, the same counters for every derived layer, a reproducible per-call manifest (prompt hash, tokenizer, cache state, tokens, retries, queue delay), or that manifest plus an enforced write token budget per namespace?
today: window_stats (about 40 counters) for call 1 (engine.py:13788) and model_usage per role (engine.py:13257); sleep layers lack failure and grounding counters (G-W13); token counts 309/353/958 are historical, not reproduced (RV10).
others: LightMem reports per-stage calls and tokens; Nemori accounts per phase with a hard token budget (TokenBudgetExceeded); Honcho logs per-call token telemetry; Hindsight keeps a cached system prefix with provider breakpoints (G-W45).

options.label: Call-1 counters (today)
options.detail: Window counters and per-role usage.
options.note: Blind to sleep-layer cost and failures.

options.label: Per-layer counters
options.detail: Calls, tokens, failures and ungrounded items for every derived layer.
options.note: Comparable layers; no reproducibility guarantee.

options.label: Reproducible call manifest
options.detail: B plus per call: rendered prompt hash, tokenizer and template, prefix-cache state, input/output tokens, retries, queue delay, p50/p95 turn-to-searchable.
options.note: Cost claims become checkable; feeds prompt-cache work.

options.label: C plus enforced budget
options.detail: Optional token or call budget per namespace and period; when spent, extraction pauses and sources are marked underived (no loss).
options.note: Hard cost ceiling for hosted models; freshness drops when hit.

why: RV10 and RV20 require reproducible manifests and stage labels before any token or latency claim; a budget that pauses (not drops) reuses the underived state from W-25 and matters once a hosted extractor is bound. Budget off by default.

title: Source of truth for memory
question: What is the single authoritative copy of memory from which every other store is rebuilt?
today: One append-only memory_events log (SQLite or Postgres) with rebuildable projections for records, vectors, BM25 and graph; log mode full/rolling/ephemeral (core/events.py:33-48, config/schema.py:43 EventLogConfig, StorageConfig:79). BD-3 keeps Markdown out as truth.
others: Hindsight and Honcho: Postgres tables are truth, vectors synced by a reconciler. EverMemOS: Markdown + YAML files are truth, SQLite and LanceDB are derived and disposable. MemOS and Graphiti (combined): the graph DB node store is truth, raw turns not durable. Mem0: the vector payload is the only copy.

options.label: Event log + projections (today)
options.detail: Every change is an event; tables, vectors, lexical and graph are replayed projections with high-water marks.
options.note: Best audit, replay and erasure proof; replay cost grows with history.

options.label: Relational tables as truth
options.detail: Current-state tables with a separate history table; vectors and graph synced from them.
options.note: Simpler queries and ops; audit, replay and taint tracing must be rebuilt by hand.

options.label: Markdown files as truth (BD-3)
options.detail: Human-editable files per user/episode; indexes rebuilt from files.
options.note: Hand-editable and portable; no reliable lineage, erasure cascade or concurrent-writer safety.

options.label: Graph database as truth
options.detail: Nodes and edges are the canonical memory; raw turns optional.
options.note: Rich structure; a failed extraction loses evidence and the graph shape is locked in.

options.label: Event log + derived Markdown export view
options.detail: Keep A as truth; add a one-way (or reviewed two-way) Markdown view per namespace whose edits re-enter as ordinary writes.
options.note: Gains readability without giving up audit; edits must pass the write door like any other input.

why: BD-3 already decided the log beats files for audit, erasure cascades and replay; RV19 and RV21 show the engines that drop raw input (MemOS, Nemori, LightMem) lose evidence on failure. An export view costs little and covers the human-editing use case.

paper.layer: all types (L0 raw is the log)

title: Derived layer stack L0-L5
question: How should v2 organise derived memory into layers (raw, assertions, episodes/summaries, graph/temporal, observations/profile, standing answers) and where does each layer live?
today: Layers are implicit: memory_type plus source.channel/tags distinguish raw turns, window facts (channel window), summaries, list cards and edges, all as MemoryRecord rows in one read model (core/records.py:174 'Memory-type packages specialize behaviour, not shape').
others: MIRIX: one Postgres table per memory type. Hindsight: facts and observations share one table split by fact_type. Graphiti (combined): episodes, entities and edges as separate graph node/edge kinds. Mnemon: raw journal plus one consolidated index overlay.

options.label: Implicit layers (today)
options.detail: One universal record; layer inferred from channel, tags and memory type.
options.note: No schema change; layer rules scattered across channels and tags.

options.label: Explicit layer field on one record shape
options.detail: Add layer in {L0..L5} and a derivation-policy version to every record; one store, per-layer indexes and budgets.
options.note: Clear read budgets and erasure scope per layer without new stores (review: labels are a taxonomy, not six storage systems).

options.label: Separate table/store per layer
options.detail: Typed tables per layer with layer-specific columns.
options.note: Typed columns; cross-layer ranking, lineage and migrations get harder.

options.label: Two layers only (raw + facts)
options.detail: Drop summaries, graph and observations; rely on raw evidence and atomic facts.
options.note: Cheapest; loses navigation, value histories and profile features.

why: The review's layer table (L0 raw ... L5 standing) maps every open gap to a layer and warns it is not six stores; an explicit field lets the token budget (G-W25) and erasure cascade reason per layer without a storage split.

title: Which memory types v2 keeps
question: Which of the nine memory types stay first-class in v2, and how does each map onto a layer and a store?
today: Nine type packages (memories/{working,episodic,semantic,procedural,reflective,resource,associative,prospective,shared}); base template enables working, episodic and semantic only (config/templates/base.yaml:42-47); others are template opt-ins.
others: MIRIX: six typed stores (core, episodic, semantic, procedural, resource, knowledge vault) each with its own agent. Hindsight: world vs experience facts, observations, mental models. Honcho: messages and conclusions (explicit/deductive/inductive). Mem0: one fact type.

options.label: Keep nine packages as today
options.detail: Nine engine types, three on in base.
options.note: Matches the paper vocabulary; many rarely used code paths to maintain.

options.label: Nine as a type tag, mapped to layers
options.detail: Keep the nine names as a record type; fix one mapping: working=context, episodic=L0/L2, semantic=L1, associative=L3 projection, reflective=L4, procedural/prospective=L5, resource=L0 documents; shared becomes a mechanism (grants), not a type.
options.note: Paper and engine say the same thing; associative and shared stop being separate stores.

options.label: Four core types, rest as features
options.detail: working, episodic, semantic, procedural only; reflection, prospective and sharing become features over them.
options.note: Lean engine; drifts from the paper's nine-type map.

options.label: Agent-per-type stores
options.detail: Each type owned by its own extraction agent and table.
options.note: Strong typing; many LLM calls and cross-type duplication.

why: The type-to-layer mapping removes the two store-like types that are really mechanisms (associative = graph projection, shared = grants, namespace.py:56) while keeping the paper's nine-type vocabulary.

title: Storage backend profile
question: Which physical stores does v2 support for the log, records, vectors, lexical index and graph?
today: Log and read model in SQLite (default) or Postgres (config/schema.py:88); LanceDB is the sole vector store (VectorConfig:139); Tantivy BM25 is core (ReadConfig lexical_provider); graph LadybugDB when installed else SQLite adjacency (GraphConfig:186). Postgres keeps Lance/Tantivy files in data_dir.
others: Hindsight and MIRIX: Postgres only (pgvector + tsvector). Cognee: SQLite + LanceDB + Ladybug by default, Postgres/pgvector/Neo4j adapters. Mem0: Qdrant + SQLite history. Graphiti (combined): Neo4j + Weaviate + Postgres.

options.label: Embedded polyglot (today)
options.detail: SQLite/Postgres + LanceDB + Tantivy + Ladybug/SQLite graph, all rebuilt from the log.
options.note: Zero-server default; four stores to keep consistent and erase from.

options.label: Postgres-only server profile
options.detail: pgvector for vectors, Postgres FTS for lexical, SQL tables for graph; one transaction covers log and projections.
options.note: Transactional erasure and backups; needs a server, BM25 quality weaker than Tantivy.

options.label: Two profiles from one log
options.detail: Embedded (SQLite + LanceDB + Tantivy + Ladybug) and server (Postgres + pgvector + FTS + SQL graph), both pure projections of the same event schema.
options.note: Covers laptop and multi-user deployments; two projection sets to test.

options.label: Single embedded multimodal store
options.detail: LanceDB for records, vectors and FTS together; graph in LanceDB tables.
options.note: Fewest moving parts; weaker lexical and graph features.

why: Postgres today still writes Lance/Tantivy files outside the database, so encryption (ADR-035) and erasure proof cover only part of the data (ADR-039 lexical residue). A server profile that keeps everything in Postgres closes that while the embedded profile stays the default.

title: Isolation and tenancy model
question: What is the isolation unit (tenant, user, agent, session) and how is it enforced in every store and key?
today: Hierarchical namespace path, max 16 segments, the one isolation boundary (core/namespace.py:25); group_id and tags are filters, not security (core/records.py:191-197); vectors share one table with a namespace prefilter unless vector.isolation=per_namespace (config/schema.py:170); session_key/source_role columns (alembic 0005).
others: Mem0: user_id/agent_id/run_id, at least one required. MIRIX: organisation > client > user with read/write scopes on every row. Cognee: per-dataset ACL and one graph+vector DB per dataset. EverMemOS: app/project/owner, with index rows keyed without project (RV21 conditional risk).

options.label: Namespace path, shared tables (today)
options.detail: One path string; prefilter in shared physical tables.
options.note: Simple; isolation rests on every query carrying the prefilter.

options.label: Typed scope tuple on every row and key
options.detail: Explicit tenant/user/agent/session columns, all included in every identity key, cache key and index key; namespace path derived from them.
options.note: Prevents the key-omits-scope class of bug (RV07, RV21); more columns.

options.label: Physical partition per user
options.detail: Per-namespace vector tables (I4) and per-namespace graph/lexical; erase drops the partition.
options.note: Strongest isolation and erasure; many small tables at scale.

options.label: Database per tenant
options.detail: One database (or schema) per tenant, shared tables inside.
options.note: Clean tenant boundary; cross-tenant ops and migrations multiply.

why: RV07 and RV21 both trace risk to identity or cache keys that omit part of the scope; a typed tuple included in every key makes that checkable, and C/D stay deployment options on top.

title: Assertion envelope on records
question: Should a derived fact be a free-text record with an (entity, attribute) key, or a versioned assertion envelope with typed value, evidence, assertor, modality and times?
today: MemoryRecord carries content text, optional (entity, attribute) key and free tags (core/records.py:183-197); window facts ignore speaker/subject/confidence on deposit (RV03, workers/windows.py:829).
others: Graphiti (combined): edge with fact text, endpoints, episode list and four timestamps. Hindsight: narrative fact with what/when/where/who/why fields and occurred_start/end. Memori: subject/predicate/object rows. Cognee: typed Pydantic DataPoints with source_* fields.

options.label: Text + key + tags (today)
options.detail: Keep the universal record; extra semantics live in tags.
options.note: Flexible; fields have no guaranteed consumer and unknown values pass silently.

options.label: Versioned assertion envelope
options.detail: text, typed value (literal/list/quantity), evidence[], assertor+subject, modality+polarity, source/event times with precision, kind+occurrence, optional graph projection, schema version; unknown enum values fail visibly.
options.note: Negation, plans and attribution survive storage and reading; every field needs a consumer (RV03).

options.label: Typed tables per fact family
options.detail: Separate typed tables (events, attributes, relations, preferences).
options.note: Strong typing; n-ary and odd facts fall between tables.

options.label: Triples only
options.detail: Every fact is subject-predicate-object.
options.note: Graph-friendly; forces fake entity nodes for lists, quantities and n-ary facts.

why: RV03 confirms fields are dropped between extraction and storage and asks for a versioned envelope with consumers; RV02 needs evidence per assertion; G-P2 needs mode/source. Literal and n-ary facts must not be forced into triples.

title: Provenance class and trust semantics
question: How should a record express where it came from and how much it is trusted?
today: SourceInfo has free-text role and channel, prompt_version, principal and parents (core/records.py:111-128); a scalar trust in [0,1] with quarantine and corroborations (records.py:231-234); derivations take the minimum parent trust. No closed class for user_stated / assistant_proposed / user_confirmed.
others: Mem0: attributed_to user or assistant. Hindsight: world vs experience facts and observation proof_count. Cognee: source_pipeline/task/user/content_hash, no trust. Honcho: conclusion level explicit/deductive/inductive.

options.label: Free role/channel + scalar trust (today)
options.detail: Keep strings and one trust number.
options.note: Works; the paper's src(m) has no enforced value set.

options.label: Closed provenance class + class trust cap
options.detail: src(m) in {user_stated, assistant_proposed, user_confirmed, tool, document, external, derived}; trust capped per class; assistant_proposed never becomes user fact without explicit assent.
options.note: Stops assistant suggestions turning into user facts (sycophancy loop); needs extractor support.

options.label: Class + proof count
options.detail: B plus a support count of independent sources per record.
options.note: Lets reinforcement raise confidence without overriding provenance.

options.label: Metadata only, no trust
options.detail: Rich source fields, no trust arithmetic.
options.note: Simple; no basis for the firewall's reach bound.

why: The paper already defines src(m) and tau_m (G1) and N1 depends on trust caps; G-P2 asks for source classes, and G-W40 wants reinforcement counts. corroborations already exists, so C mainly closes the class set.

title: Speaker, subject and asker axes
question: Where do the speaker, subject, addressee and asker axes of a record live: tags, typed columns, or separate per-observer stores?
today: Perspective layer writes tags spk:, addr:, sub:, ask:, mod:, pol:, scope:, cert:, rep: on each record, never in content (core/perspective.py:1-30); only read via tag matching behind read.perspective_mode.
others: Mem0: attributed_to only. MemMachine: producer_id / produced_for_id columns. Honcho: one collection per (observer, observed) pair. LightMem: speaker_id/name on each fact.

options.label: Tags (today)
options.detail: Prefix-tagged strings on the record.
options.note: Flexible; no index, no type checking, easy to mistype.

options.label: Typed indexed columns
options.detail: spk, sub[], addr, ask as indexed columns (entity ids where resolved), modality and polarity as enums; tags kept for free labels.
options.note: Fast filters and a stable contract; schema migration needed.

options.label: Per-observer collections
options.detail: Separate memory per (observer, observed) pair.
options.note: True theory-of-mind views; duplicates storage and extraction fan-out.

options.label: Speaker role only
options.detail: Keep user/assistant role, drop subject and asker.
options.note: Cheapest; third-party facts get attributed to the user.

why: The paper's record axes spk/sub/ask are G1 constructs; RV03 wants assertor and subject carried through storage and reading. Typed columns give them a consumer; per-observer views (C) can be derived from them later (see M-24).

title: Lineage representation
question: How should lineage from derived records back to their sources be stored and queried?
today: source.parents list on each record (core/records.py:128); WRITE/CONSOLIDATE events carry member_record_ids; erasure walks both transitively (ADR-039). No source version, no evidence span per assertion; reply-to-source window membership is process-local (RV07).
others: Honcho: document_sources table of premise to conclusion edges. Hindsight: source_memory_ids GIN-indexed plus FK cascades. EverMemOS: parent_id chain fact to episode to memcell. Graphiti (combined): edge keeps its supporting-episode list.

options.label: Parents list on the record (today)
options.detail: Forward pointers only; reverse lookup by scan or event walk.
options.note: Works; reverse lookups (what depends on X) are slow and not indexed.

options.label: Lineage edge table, indexed both ways
options.detail: (child, parent, parent_version, role) rows maintained by the projector; reverse lookup is a key read.
options.note: Fast cascades and cache invalidation; one more projection.

options.label: B + evidence spans and source versions
options.detail: Each assertion stores source id, version, line and exact span per endpoint, plus prompt/schema/model version.
options.note: Supports entailment checks, selective re-derivation and stale-cache detection; more storage.

options.label: Foreign-key cascades only
options.detail: Database FKs between tables do the work.
options.note: Simple; Nemori shows SET NULL loses sources on merge.

why: RV02 needs spans per assertion and endpoint; RV07 needs lineage that survives restart and carries source/prompt/model versions; RV05 needs migration aliases. The current parents list is kept as a field of C.

title: Temporal fields on a record
question: Which time axes does each record carry: utterance time, ingestion time, effective event interval, validity, and with what precision?
today: valid_from, valid_to, recorded_at (strictly increasing), superseded_at and invalid_at (core/records.py:199-210); coarse dates YYYY-MM/YYYY parse to day one (workers/pipelines.py:2924); happened:/said: tags carry event vs mention time.
others: Graphiti (combined): valid_at, invalid_at, created_at, expired_at on edges. Hindsight: event_date, occurred_start/end, mentioned_at, created_at. Mem0: created_at/updated_at only. EverMemOS: one timestamp, foresight has start/end.

options.label: Current bi-temporal columns (today)
options.detail: valid/recorded/superseded/invalid times; precision implicit.
options.note: Works for state changes; coarse dates claim false day-one precision.

options.label: Tri-temporal with precision
options.detail: source_time (utterance), recorded_at (ingestion), event interval [start, end] with precision (day/month/year/unknown) and uncertainty, plus validity [valid_from, valid_to) for states; plans stored as plans.
options.note: Fixes durations, coarse dates and backfilled history; more fields to populate.

options.label: Edge-only bi-temporal
options.detail: Four timestamps on graph edges, one timestamp elsewhere.
options.note: Good for the graph; facts and summaries stay single-time.

options.label: Single timestamp
options.detail: One created/observed time per record.
options.note: Simplest; no history, no as-of, wrong durations.

why: RV04 confirms utterance, ingestion and event time are conflated and coarse dates collapse to day one; G-P6 asks for spans matched by overlap. Unknown dates must remain unknown.

title: As-of read semantics
question: Which as-of questions must the store answer: what was true at time t, what did we know at time t, or both?
today: as_of_scope sets the read's point in time and filters valid_from_before = as_of (valid time only) and resolves relative phrases against it (core/read_filters.py:245-262).
others: Graphiti (combined): valid_at/invalid_at for world time and created_at/expired_at for system time, so both axes are queryable. Hindsight: occurred vs mentioned windows, no as-of. Mnemon: up to 50 earlier versions per record. Most others: no as-of.

options.label: Valid-time as-of (today)
options.detail: Answer 'what was true at t' from valid_from/valid_to.
options.note: Covers state questions; cannot reproduce what the assistant believed at t.

options.label: Two-axis as-of
options.detail: as_of_valid and as_of_known (transaction time) as separate parameters; a correction recorded later can be seen or hidden.
options.note: Enables audit replay ('why did it answer that last week') and late corrections; doubles filter logic.

options.label: Materialised snapshots
options.detail: Periodic snapshot views per namespace for fast historical reads.
options.note: Fast historical reads; storage grows and snapshots drift from the log.

options.label: Latest only
options.detail: No historical reads; superseded values are history for audit only.
options.note: Simple; loses the BD-4 value.

why: The log already holds transaction time (recorded_at, superseded_at) so B is mostly a read-filter change; it underpins audit replay and the paper's as-of read E_t = R(q_t; M, P, t_as).

title: Attribute cardinality schema
question: Where is it decided whether an attribute holds one value (supersede) or many (coexist), and how is that declared?
today: No schema: semantic records keyed (entity, attribute) go through the conflict ladder as if single-valued; edges tagged kind:event coexist; cardinality one/many/count exists only in the read-side query contract (core/query_contract.py:92).
others: Cognee: caller-declared functional relationships keep the newest and tag older ones. Mem0 and MIRIX: the LLM decides update vs add per write. Mnemon: value keys with dated history and a conflict flag. Honcho: card prefixes only.

options.label: Implicit by kind (today)
options.detail: state = single, event = many, decided by extractor kind.
options.note: Lists (pets, children, cities lived in) get superseded by mistake.

options.label: Declared attribute registry with defaults
options.detail: Registry attribute -> cardinality one/many, functional flag and exclusivity, with built-in defaults and per-namespace overrides; unknown attributes default to many (coexist) until a rule says otherwise.
options.note: Deterministic, auditable supersede; registry needs upkeep across domains.

options.label: Extractor emits cardinality per fact
options.detail: The write prompt labels each fact single/multi.
options.note: No registry; model errors become wrong supersedes.

options.label: LLM decides at write
options.detail: Update/add/delete decided per incoming fact by an LLM over neighbours.
options.note: Adaptive; non-deterministic and destructive.

why: CLAUDE.md G0 makes cardinality a schema property; a registry gives the conflict ladder a deterministic rule while C can propose new entries for review. Defaulting unknown attributes to coexist avoids silent loss.

title: Value histories and observations
question: How should changing values and recurring patterns be represented: archived versions on a record, value-history lines, or consolidated observations?
today: Superseded records keep history (ArchivedVersion list, core/records.py:165, 216) and superseded_at; conflict ladder supersede/contest; corroborations count; list cards per (person, class) (ADR-044); no observation layer (G-W29 missing).
others: Mnemon: per key a dated value list with conflict flag. Hindsight: observations with proof_count, history and staleness, consolidated by LLM per 8 facts. LightMem: offline similarity-gated update. Memori: num_times on repeated facts.

options.label: Archived versions per record (today)
options.detail: Each keyed record carries its own superseded versions.
options.note: History exists but is scattered across records.

options.label: Value-history line per (subject, attribute)
options.detail: One derived record listing dated values with conflict flag and pointers to source facts.
options.note: Compact 'how did X change' answers; derived and must cascade on erase.

options.label: Observations with proof counts
options.detail: Consolidated beliefs over unkeyed facts with support count, history and staleness.
options.note: Fewer tokens in context; LLM consolidation cost and drift risk.

options.label: B for keyed state + C for patterns
options.detail: Value lines for single-valued attributes, observations for many-valued and behavioural patterns, both citing facts.
options.note: Most complete; two derived record kinds to maintain.

why: G-W29 proposes exactly this split (group by (subject, attribute) and by similarity) with only changed groups reaching the LLM; synthesis puts observations at L4 replacing covered raw facts in context.

title: Episodes, sessions and sagas
question: What are the grouping units above a turn (episode, session, thread/saga), and are they records with membership?
today: Session = caller-stamped session_id stored in source.message_id, passive lifecycle (ADR-037); session summaries per closed session (ADR-048); episode fragments in window mode all, off (workers/windows.py:883); no thread or saga object.
others: Graphiti (combined): every thread is a Saga with HAS_EPISODE and previous-episode chain. Nemori and EverMemOS: topic episodes are the retrieved unit. Honcho: workspace > peer > session. Hindsight: no sessions, documents and chunks.

options.label: Session id + session summary (today)
options.detail: Session is a label; summary and lifecycle per session.
options.note: Simple; topic boundaries inside a session invisible.

options.label: Turn -> episode -> session -> saga records
options.detail: Explicit membership records at each level; episodes from topic segmentation, sagas link sessions on the same thread or goal across time.
options.note: Navigation and multi-session tasks; segmentation errors propagate.

options.label: Episodes only
options.detail: Topic episodes replace sessions as the unit.
options.note: Good retrieval unit; loses caller session semantics.

options.label: No grouping
options.detail: Flat records plus documents.
options.note: Least work; no session-level summaries or lifecycle.

why: G-W1 and G-CALL2 need episode and stitched-narrative units; agent workloads need a cross-session saga (task thread). Membership records keep erasure cascades exact.

title: Entity identity model
question: How is an entity identified, aliased, typed and merged, and can merges be undone?
today: Entity id derives from canonical name (ADR-064: 'an entity id derives from its canonical name'); resolution ladder off by default (exact, alias, embedding top-15, entropy gate, MinHash >= 0.9; memories/associative/resolution.py).
others: Cognee: deterministic id from lower-cased name, chunk-scoped when types differ. Graphiti (combined): uuid nodes, MinHash then LLM dedupe for unresolved names. Hindsight: pg_trgm candidates with word compatibility, no LLM. Mem0: exact text or cosine >= 0.95.

options.label: Name-derived id (today)
options.detail: id = hash(namespace, canonical name).
options.note: Cheap and stable; homonyms merge, renames split.

options.label: Opaque id + alias table + type + scope
options.detail: Entity row with uuid, type, aliases, scope; merges and splits are logged events, reversible; ambiguous mentions stay unresolved.
options.note: Handles homonyms and renames; needs calibrated thresholds per mechanism.

options.label: No entities
options.detail: Names stay in text.
options.note: Simplest; no entity leg or per-entity views.

options.label: Caller-declared peers only
options.detail: Only participants the client declares are entities.
options.note: Safe; third parties unmodelled.

why: RV17: name MinHash and embedding thresholds are different mechanisms and the same name can be different people; no auto-merge on spelling alone. Reversible merge events keep the log as truth.

title: Relation and edge representation
question: Are relations stored as their own edges, as keyed semantic records, or as assertion nodes with role edges for n-ary facts?
today: Each edge (src, rel, dst, fact) becomes a semantic record keyed (entity=src, attribute=rel) with kind:/rel:/dst: tags and a LINK event to its source; the graph store is only a projection of LINK events (core/events.py:57-61).
others: Graphiti (combined): RELATES_TO edges with fact text, embedding, episode list and bi-temporal fields. Hindsight: untyped fact-to-fact links (temporal, semantic, caused_by). Memori: SQL subject/predicate/object rows. Cognee: free snake_case edge names with edge_text.

options.label: Edges as keyed semantic records (today)
options.detail: One record per edge; graph is a projection.
options.note: Uniform with facts; binary only, endpoint roles in tags.

options.label: First-class edge objects
options.detail: Typed edge rows with occurrence, evidence list and four timestamps.
options.note: Rich graph semantics; a second fact store to keep consistent with records.

options.label: Assertion-centric with reified n-ary nodes
options.detail: The assertion envelope is truth; binary edges are compiled from it; facts with more than two roles keep an event/assertion node with role edges.
options.note: No fake entities, one truth; projection logic more complex.

options.label: Untyped record links
options.detail: Links between facts (temporal, semantic, causal) instead of relations.
options.note: Cheap; no relation queries.
