why: RV03 says compile optional graph edges from a versioned assertion envelope and keep relations with more than two roles as an event/assertion node; it also keeps the log-as-truth model (graph = projection).

title: Assertion and edge identity key
question: What key decides that two extracted assertions are the same fact, the same event occurrence, or a new one?
today: _edge_key keys (ns, src, rel, dst) without kind; dated events add day and numerals; an archived key short-circuits before the conflict ladder, so A->B->A is skipped (workers/pipelines.py:1882-1895, G-W50).
others: Graphiti (combined): every edge occurrence has its own uuid and an episode list; duplicates judged per fact with numeric and date qualifiers. Memori: sha256 of normalised text, repeats bump num_times. Mem0: MD5 text match on neighbours.

options.label: Triple key, day for dated events (today)
options.detail: (ns, src, rel, dst) [+ day, numbers].
options.note: Collapses same-day repeats and blocks state returns.

options.label: Versioned key with kind and occurrence
options.detail: (scope, src, rel, dst, kind) + occurrence id from cited source turns for events; archived keys go to the ladder; key version stored with old-key aliases for migration.
options.note: Fixes A-B-A and repeated events; needs a migration of existing keys.

options.label: uuid per occurrence + semantic dedup
options.detail: Every extraction is new; a resolver merges re-mentions into one occurrence and appends provenance.
options.note: Most accurate; resolver calls and thresholds.

options.label: Content hash only
options.detail: Normalised text hash decides identity.
options.note: Cheap; paraphrases duplicate and different events collide.

why: G-W50 is a prerequisite for online graph deposit (G-W49); RV05 asks to separate assertion identity, event occurrence and semantic dedup and to define migration with old-key aliases. C's resolver can sit on top for ambiguous cases.

title: Graph store backend
question: Which engine stores the graph projection by default, and what must any backend support?
today: graph.provider auto = LadybugDB when installed else SQLite adjacency; neo4j available; kuzu deprecated (config/schema.py:186, ADR-064); LadybugDB used without HNSW because of three crashes; graph built only when associative memory is on.
others: Cognee: embedded Ladybug by default, Neo4j/Neptune/Kuzu adapters. Hindsight: no graph DB, graph lives in Postgres tables. Graphiti (combined) and MemOS: Neo4j server. Memori: SQL triple tables.

options.label: Auto Ladybug else SQL adjacency (today)
options.detail: Embedded graph DB when installed.
options.note: Cypher and native FTS; young engine with crash workarounds.

options.label: SQL tables in the main store
options.detail: Entities, edges and adjacency as tables beside the read model; same transaction and backup as the log projection.
options.note: Transactional with the outbox (RV06); multi-hop traversal slower.

options.label: Neo4j / server graph
options.detail: External graph server.
options.note: Mature traversal and algorithms; another server and erasure surface.

options.label: Pluggable with a capability contract
options.detail: Keep the projection interface; any backend must pass isolation, erasure and rebuild tests; default chosen per storage profile (embedded: Ladybug, server: SQL tables).
options.note: Fits M-04 profiles; contract tests to maintain.

why: The graph is a projection of LINK events, so the backend is swappable; RV06 wants transactional projection recovery and RV21 wants isolation and erasure tests per store. A capability contract makes that explicit.

title: Community and cluster layer
question: Should v2 keep graph communities with summary parents, and how are they kept stable over time?
today: reorganize sleep stage: Leiden (graspologic, warm-started) + LPA refinement or LPA alone with collapse guard; communities >= 3 get a summary parent; partition stored as MARKER deltas so rebuild reproduces it (ADR-043).
others: Graphiti (combined): label propagation once a user has 5+ entities, 24 h cooldown, off by default. MemOS: recursive MiniBatchKMeans with LLM summary parents, off by default. EverMemOS: episode clustering at cosine 0.65 within 7 days. Hindsight: none, observation scopes instead.

options.label: Leiden + LPA hybrid, opt-in (today)
options.detail: Graph communities with summary parents.
options.note: Deterministic and rebuildable; unmeasured benefit on real memory graphs.

options.label: Embedding clusters of episodes
options.detail: Cluster episodes or facts by vector similarity in a time window.
options.note: No graph needed; clusters ignore relations.

options.label: Hierarchical multi-level communities
options.detail: Several community levels with summaries per level for global questions.
options.note: Answers corpus-wide questions; heavy summarisation cost.

options.label: Drop communities
options.detail: Use observation scopes and entity summaries instead.
options.note: Less code; loses topic-level navigation.

why: ADR-043 already made partitions deterministic and replayable; no benchmark in scope shows a gain, so keep it opt-in and calibrate on real graphs (KB-8) before investing in hierarchy.

answer.note: A + D add extra, not remove Commodities

title: Profile and persona representation
question: Is the user profile a capped typed card, a query over facts, a free-text summary, or a caller-set persona?
today: Persona is a caller-set working record pinned first and never paged (memories/working/persona.py:17, paging.py:13); reflect_profile and profile_header_packing are off (config/schema.py:777); no card schema or caps (G-W30 built-off).
others: Honcho: peer card with four prefixes, 200 chars per entry, 40 entries, enforced in code. MIRIX: 'human' and 'persona' core blocks, 5,000 chars, always injected. Hindsight: a standing question ('what are this user's preferences') answered and refreshed. EverMemOS: explicit_info + implicit_traits, 60 items, 8 per category.

options.label: Caller persona + optional insights (today)
options.detail: Persona set by caller; derived insights in reflective memory, off.
options.note: No profile leakage; no learned profile either.

options.label: Capped typed card citing facts
options.detail: Entries typed identity / attribute / relationship / instruction, code-enforced caps, stated-only by default, each entry points to its source facts, relevance-gated injection.
options.note: Compact and auditable; must not leak into unrelated answers.

options.label: Profile as a query over facts
options.detail: No stored card; profile assembled on demand from facts about the user.
options.note: Never stale; costs a retrieval each time.

options.label: Free-text block always injected
options.detail: One rewritten summary or core block in every prompt.
options.note: Simple; leaks into unrelated answers and hides provenance.

why: G-W30 proposes a typed capped card and the OP-Bench lesson is that profiles leak into unrelated answers, so relevance gating and fact pointers (for erasure cascade) are required; the caller persona stays as a separate pinned block.

title: Working memory and context state
question: Is working memory persisted as records, rebuilt per turn, or held as a rolling summary or KV-cache?
today: Working records live in the store; MemGPT-style paging evicts oldest unpinned records beyond page_size (memories/working/paging.py:13-21); persona pinned; no KV-cache memory (BD-7).
others: MemMachine: in-process deque of recent episodes plus a rolling LLM summary of evicted turns, persisted per session. MIRIX: agents summarise their own history at 75% context pressure. MemOS: activation (KV) memory prefilled into vLLM/HF caches. Honcho: rolling short and long session summaries.

options.label: Persisted working records with paging (today)
options.detail: Hot window as records; evicted records page out through the write door.
options.note: Auditable; working state is mixed into the long-term store.

options.label: Ephemeral per-turn context
options.detail: M_ctx rebuilt each turn from history and retrieval; nothing persisted except turns.
options.note: Matches the paper default (M_ctx rebuilt per turn); no carry-over of scratch state.

options.label: A + rolling summary of evicted turns
options.detail: Paged-out turns are folded into a per-session rolling summary that stays in context.
options.note: Long sessions stay coherent; one summarise call per eviction batch.

options.label: KV-cache activation memory
options.detail: Prefill stable blocks (persona, card) into a reusable KV cache.
options.note: Big latency win; needs an in-process model (BD-7).

why: Long agent sessions overflow the window; MemMachine and Honcho keep evicted turns as a rolling summary, and ADR-048 already has the incremental summarise prompt. KV memory stays later until the llama.cpp in-process adapter (BD-7).

title: Compressed multi-resolution representations
question: How should higher layers store compressed forms of lower-layer content so the reader can trade tokens for detail?
today: Each layer stores full text; window facts copy text; episode summary not attached (RV09); cold tier zstd-compresses content bytes (core/records.py:244-245), which saves disk, not tokens; read.gist_after exists (config/schema.py:1007).
others: MemOS and Memori: window or conversation summary stored once and attached to facts. LightMem: LLMLingua-2 compresses each message 20-40% and overwrites it in place. Mnemon: pointer-style items back to record ids. Hindsight: chunks returned on request (include.chunks).

options.label: Full text per layer (today)
options.detail: No token-level compression; byte compression in cold tier.
options.note: Simple; duplicated text across layers costs tokens.

options.label: Summary once + pointers
options.detail: Each compact unit stores its text once and points to parents; facts reference their window summary instead of copying it.
options.note: Fewer tokens and no stale copies (RV09).

options.label: Token-compressed text stored
options.detail: Store LLMLingua-style compressed text as a layer beside (never instead of) raw.
options.note: 20-40% fewer tokens; can drop needed detail (G-W31).

options.label: Multi-resolution per record
options.detail: Every derived unit carries gist (one line), note (about 50 tokens) and full pointer; the reader picks a level per budget.
options.note: Budget-aware reading; three texts to keep consistent.

options.label: Learned soft/gist tokens
options.detail: Store learned compressed embeddings (gist tokens) consumed by the generator.
options.note: Large savings; model-specific and not inspectable.

why: RV09 asks to store summaries once with a pointer; the synthesis budget design uses pointer notes and G-W41 two read tiers. D generalises B; raw stays authoritative so C is only an optional extra level.

title: Embedding model and multi-vector
question: Which embedding representation does a record get: one vector from a small English model, a multilingual default, or several named vectors per record?
today: fastembed BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5, 384-d, by default (config/schema.py:104); one vector per record in a LanceDB table per embedder_id (services/vector/lancedb_store.py:27); entity-name vectors optional in the graph store (ADR-064); anticipatory cues are separate records with a token-overlap encoder (services/query_encoder/cues.py).
others: Hindsight: bge-small-en default with a multilingual-e5-small option. EverMemOS: Qwen3-Embedding-4B truncated to 1,024-d; episode body and subject embedded separately. Cognee: several indexed fields (entity name, chunk text, summary, edge name). Honcho/Mem0: text-embedding-3-small.

options.label: One small English vector (today)
options.detail: Single 384-d vector per record.
options.note: Fast on CPU; weak on non-English and long content.

options.label: Multilingual default, one vector
options.detail: Swap the default to a small multilingual model; English model as preset.
options.note: Generic across languages; re-embed on switch (rebuild from log).

options.label: Named multi-vectors per record
options.detail: content + question/cue view + entity/subject vector per record, each its own column/index, fused at read.
options.note: Better recall for paraphrased questions; more index space and write time.

options.label: Late interaction (token vectors)
options.detail: ColBERT-style multi-vector per token for rescoring.
options.note: Best fine-grained matching; heavy storage.

options.label: Matryoshka / quantised two-stage
options.detail: Truncated or int8 vectors for prefilter, full for rescore (E4 seam exists).
options.note: Scale aid, not a quality change.

why: Generic workloads include non-English users (non_english preset); a multilingual default is a config change with log rebuild. Named multi-vectors (C) are the advanced step once the cue and entity legs prove value.

title: Shared memory and per-observer views
question: How do several agents or users share memory: type-scoped grants, a shared bank, scoped read/write lists, or per-observer views?
today: Revocable grants by memory type, checked only in grant_allows (core/namespace.py:56-82); foreign records capped at trust 0.3 (or trust x kappa with integrity); shared off in base, on in the multi_agent template; per-observer views missing (G-W48 partial via perspective tags).
others: Honcho: one collection per (observer, observed) pair, fanned out from one extraction. MIRIX: per-client write_scope and read_scopes over one user store. Hindsight: several agents write one bank, tags scope visibility. Cognee: dataset 'share' permission.

options.label: Type-scoped grants with trust cap (today)
options.detail: Pull-only grants, foreign trust capped.
options.note: Supports the N1 reach bound; coarse (whole type).

options.label: Shared bank with tags
options.detail: Agents write into one store; tags scope reads.
options.note: Easy collaboration; no per-agent trust, poisoning spreads.

options.label: A + derived per-observer views
options.detail: Keep grants; add a derived 'about X as seen by Y' view built from speaker/subject axes at sleep.
options.note: Theory-of-mind for multi-agent; extra derived records.

options.label: Read/write scope lists per agent
options.detail: Every record has a write scope; agents read a list of scopes.
options.note: Flexible; MIRIX shows paths that skip the scope filter.

why: Grants are the base of N1 (proved cross-agent reach bound) and should stay; G-W48 proposes per-observer views derived from perspective tags, which M-08 makes typed columns.

title: Forgetting and erasure of derived text
question: When a source is forgotten, what happens to derived text (summaries, cards, observations, edges) and to residual copies in caches and indexes?
today: Soft forget by default; hard forget cascades transitively through source.parents and members, deletes (not re-derives) summaries, redacts log payloads, purges caches and old LanceDB versions; Tantivy terms remain until segment merge (residual_risks, engine.py:10321; ADR-039; core/erasure.py).
others: Hindsight: deleting a document cascades to observations and resets surviving facts for re-consolidation. MemMachine: profile features survive deletion of their source episode. Mem0: history table keeps deleted text. Cognee: forget removes derived graph/vector artefacts via chunk-scoped ownership refs.

options.label: Cascade delete derived (today)
options.detail: Any derived record that touched the source is deleted, not rebuilt.
options.note: Provable; loses unrelated content of large summaries.

options.label: Cascade + deferred re-derivation
options.detail: Delete affected derived records at once, then queue re-derivation from surviving sources off the erasure path, with a generation check so stale results never publish.
options.note: Keeps memory useful after erasure; re-derivation cost and tombstone checks.

options.label: Crypto-shredding per subject
options.detail: Encrypt payloads per subject key; erasure destroys the key so log, backups and residual index files become unreadable.
options.note: Covers backups and lexical residue; key management burden.

options.label: Soft delete with retention purge
options.detail: Hide on forget, purge on a schedule.
options.note: Cheap; derived text survives until purge.

why: ADR-039 rejected re-derivation on the erasure path, not afterwards; RV07 asks for tombstones and generation checks so a forget during inference never republishes. C is worth an ADR for the regulated template because lexical residue is unproven today.

title: Schema versioning and migration
question: How do the event schema, record schema and derived layers evolve across versions without losing or duplicating memory?
today: Events carry schema_version = 1 (core/events.py:122); SQLite read model uses Alembic migrations 0001-0005 (services/storage/sqlite/alembic/versions); Postgres Alembic tree is a documented follow-up (ADR-025); projections rebuild from the log; derived records keep prompt_version only.
others: Hindsight: Alembic migrations on Postgres including dropped entity edges. Nemori: migration 4 dropped pgvector columns for Qdrant. Graphiti (combined): offline migration jobs only. Mnemon: versioned JSON formats (mnemon-records/v1).

options.label: Alembic + projection rebuild (today)
options.detail: Migrate the read model, rebuild projections; events stay at v1.
options.note: Works while the event schema is frozen.

options.label: Event upcasters + derivation versions
options.detail: Each event kind has a schema_version and an upcaster chain; every derived record stores derivation policy (prompt, schema, model, key version), so a change re-derives only affected records; old keys keep aliases.
options.note: Safe evolution of the assertion envelope and keys; upcaster tests per version.

options.label: In-place data migrations
options.detail: Rewrite stored payloads to the new schema.
options.note: Simple; breaks log immutability and audit hash chain.

options.label: Re-ingest from raw on change
options.detail: Drop derived layers and re-extract everything.
options.note: Clean; full LLM cost every schema change.

why: v2 changes the assertion envelope (M-06), keys (M-17) and time fields (M-10); RV05 requires no duplicated facts on migration with old-key aliases and RV07 requires cache identity by prompt/schema/model. Upcasters keep the audit chain (ADR-042) intact.

title: Where offline derivation runs
question: Should offline derivation stay one monolithic sleep cycle, or be split into tiers by when the evidence is complete (session close versus background sleep) with each artefact owned by exactly one tier?
today: One ordered sleep() pass (workers/schedule.py:29-51, 13 stages plus up to 4 conditional) does everything; the session-close hook exists but is a stub (workers/pipelines.py:3669, engine.py:13754); call 1 runs per window when write.window_extract is on (ADR-066).
others: Honcho: a Postgres task queue with typed tasks (summary, representation, dream, deletion, reconciler) consumed by deriver workers. Hindsight: consolidation job after every retain plus a 300 s reconcile loop and mental-model refresh ticks. EverMemOS: Offline Memory Engine with per-strategy Immediate / Cron / Idle / Counter triggers. Cognee: improve() runs nine gated stages after a session remember().

options.label: Monolithic sleep (today)
options.detail: Every derived layer is produced by one ordered pass that the caller (or an interval timer) starts.
options.note: Simple and deterministic, but session-level artefacts wait for the next sleep and every stage rescans every namespace.

options.label: Three tiers: window, session close, sleep
options.detail: Call 1 per window (facts, edges), call 2 once per closed session (summary, stitched episode, profile ops), call 3 in the background (resolution, invalidation, observations, communities, decay); each artefact has one owning tier.
options.note: Fresher session artefacts and smaller sleep passes, at the price of a second scheduling path to test.

options.label: Typed task queue per artefact
options.detail: Each derivation is a persisted task type with its own trigger, retry and dead-letter; sleep becomes just one task family.
options.note: Most flexible and scalable; needs a queue backend and per-task idempotence everywhere.

options.label: Event-driven after every write
options.detail: Consolidation reacts to each deposit immediately on the touched neighbourhood.
options.note: Freshest, but LLM cost scales with write rate and runs race each other.

why: ADR-066 already fixes the call 1 / call 2 / call 3 split and G-CALL2 is the missing middle tier; tiers keep the zero-LLM hot path while letting session artefacts land at close. A typed queue (C) can come later on top of the durable-derivation work of RV01.

title: Sleep trigger policy
question: What should start a background (call 3) cycle for a namespace: an explicit call, a fixed interval, accumulated volume and idleness with a minimum spacing, or every deposit?
today: sleep() runs only when called (engine.py:13314); SleepScheduler (workers/scheduler.py:38) runs the whole cycle on a fixed interval but workers.sleep_interval_seconds defaults to None (config/schema.py:285); ConsolidationTrigger.HEAT exists but is unwired and warns (workers/pipelines.py:416).
others: Honcho: dream once 50 new conclusions accrue, newest 60 min old, at most every 8 h. Hindsight: after every retain, delete or update. EverMemOS: Immediate, Cron, Idle and Counter triggers per strategy. memU: host agent runs headless every 60 min. MIRIX: skill evolution every 5 sealed task sessions.

options.label: Explicit call only (today)
options.detail: The host calls sleep(); nothing runs by itself.
options.note: Deterministic for evals, but derived layers go stale in any long-lived deployment that forgets to call it.

options.label: Fixed interval
options.detail: Run the cycle every N seconds regardless of activity (the existing scheduler switched on).
options.note: Wastes cycles on idle namespaces and lags busy ones.

options.label: Volume + idle + minimum spacing per namespace
options.detail: Fire when a namespace gains N new deposits AND has been idle M minutes, never more often than every K hours; manual sleep() still works and shares the same lock.
options.note: Work tracks real change and avoids running mid-conversation; three knobs to tune per workload.

options.label: After every deposit
options.detail: Each write schedules consolidation of what it touched.
options.note: Freshest observations, but cost proportional to write rate and constant LLM load.

why: G-W38 proposes exactly this opt-in policy with one advisory lock per namespace; off by default keeps eval runs deterministic, while long-lived assistants and agents get maintenance without a host cron.

title: Unit of work, locking and restart
question: Should a background cycle sweep every namespace globally, or run as a per-namespace job over only what changed since its watermark, and how should it resume after a crash?
today: run_sleep_cycle (workers/schedule.py:80) runs each stage across every namespace (storage.list_namespaces in each stage); manual and scheduled cycles can overlap because the cycle is global (G-W38 note); per-session stages are idempotent by done markers and membership fingerprints (stage_marker, workers/pipelines.py:2947); sleep layers have no failure counters (G-W13).
others: Honcho: per-collection dream tasks in a persisted queue, errored items kept 30 days. MIRIX: triggers claimed exactly once through a persisted cursor. Mnemon: background jobs fold the journal after a watermark. Cognee: improve() under a per-session/dataset lock.

options.label: Global sweep with done markers (today)
options.detail: Every stage scans all namespaces; idempotence comes from markers and fingerprints; a crash re-runs the cycle.
options.note: Correct but O(store) per cycle; overlapping runs need a lock that does not exist yet.

options.label: Per-namespace job, dirty set, advisory lock
options.detail: A namespace with changes since its watermark gets one job; the job takes a namespace lock, processes the changed records (and their neighbours) stage by stage, and advances the watermark only after each stage commits.
options.note: Cost proportional to change; needs dependency tracking so a resolved entity re-dirties its summaries.

options.label: Persisted leases and outbox per stage
options.detail: Each stage item is a leased task with attempts, failure reason and dead-letter; visible effects are idempotent and acknowledged after commit.
options.note: Strongest restart guarantee (RV01 gate), heaviest to build.

why: RV01 and RV07 require derived work to survive restarts without duplicate effects; per-namespace dirty sets give that with markers already in place, and G-W38 needs the shared lock anyway. Move to C if the queue backend from O-01 C is adopted.

title: Call 3 stage order
question: In what order should the background stages run, and should that order be a fixed list or a dependency graph where a stage reruns only for records an upstream stage changed?
today: Fixed SLEEP_CYCLE_ORDER (workers/schedule.py:29): consolidate, mine_facts, anticipate, reflect_profile, extract_graph, summarize_entities, reorganize, check_watches, session_lifecycle, decay_sweep, compress, sleep_compute, event_log_prune; retention_expire first, predict_calibrate / project_facts after mine_facts and rule_edges after extract_graph when on. Profile reflection runs before graph resolution and invalidation.
others: Hindsight: retain, then consolidation into observations, then mental-model refresh. Cognee: nine fixed stages (feedback_weights ... distill_sessions, update_user_preferences ... global_context_index). Graphiti / Combined: node resolution, edge dedupe and invalidation, then entity summaries, then optional communities. MIRIX: auto-dream per memory type.

options.label: Keep today's fixed order
options.detail: Profile and reflection run before the graph is reconciled.
options.note: Profile and insights can be built on facts that the same cycle later invalidates or merges.

options.label: Reconcile first, then summarise, then personalise, then maintain
options.detail: retention, reconcile online deposits and entity resolution, invalidation, dedupe, value histories and observations, entity summaries, communities, profile, reflection, standing answers, decay, compress, prune.
options.note: Every derived layer reads the reconciled state; still one list, easy to reason about.

options.label: Dependency graph with dirty propagation
options.detail: Stages declare inputs and outputs; a change in one record marks only the dependent artefacts dirty, so a quiet namespace does almost nothing.
options.note: Best incremental cost; needs lineage on every derived record (already present as source.parents).

why: ADR-066 assigns resolution and invalidation to call 3 and G-W29 / G-W39 need reconciled input; reordering is cheap and removes a correctness hazard. Adopt C once O-03 B dirty sets exist.

title: Cost caps for background work
question: How should background LLM spend be bounded: no cap, per-stage call limits, a per-namespace token budget per cycle, or a global budget with priority between stages?
today: No budget on sleep stages; window_stats counts call-1 work (engine.py window_stats) and model_usage per role, but sleep layers lack failure and grounding counters (G-W13); entity summaries skip the LLM when lines fit 2,000 chars (ENTITY_SUMMARY_FREE_CHARS, config/constants.py:439).
others: Nemori: per-phase accounting with a hard token budget. LightMem: per-stage call and token counts. Honcho: per-call token telemetry and a minimum 8 h between dreams. MIRIX: budgeted skill evolution.

options.label: No cap, counters only
options.detail: Report calls and tokens per stage; never stop work.
options.note: Visible but unbounded; a large backfill can run up a bill.

options.label: Per-stage call limit per cycle
options.detail: Each LLM stage processes at most N items per cycle, leftovers stay dirty for the next cycle.
options.note: Simple; ignores that items differ hugely in size.

options.label: Token budget per namespace per cycle, priority order
options.detail: A token budget per namespace is spent in stage priority (reconciliation before summaries before reflection); deferred work is counted and carried, never silently dropped.
options.note: Predictable spend and fairness across tenants; needs coverage-loss reporting (RV11).

options.label: Skip-if-unchanged plus free fast paths only
options.detail: Rely on fingerprints and no-call fast paths (fit-in-budget summaries, deterministic grouping) without explicit caps.
options.note: Cuts the common case but gives no upper bound.

why: G-W13 asks for the same counters on every derived layer plus an optional token budget; RV11 requires that a cap expose deferred coverage rather than discard it. Combine with D's fast paths so the budget is rarely hit.

title: Freshness guarantee for derived layers
question: What freshness contract should derived layers promise to readers: none, a reported staleness, a maximum lag bound, or read-your-writes for derived views?
today: Raw turns are readable immediately after the durable receipt; summaries, observations, entity summaries, communities and profile are as old as the last sleep() with no staleness marker; the read side cannot tell a missing derivation from a pending one.
others: Mnemon: background jobs pre-embed so no View waits, and stubs are expanded lazily. Hindsight: mental models refreshed after consolidation, read with no LLM. Combined: summaries updated after every user turn. MemMachine: ingestion poller every 2 s for sets with 5+ messages or 5 min age.

options.label: Best effort, no contract (today)
options.detail: Derived layers are whatever the last cycle produced.
options.note: A stale profile or observation can contradict a fresh raw turn with no signal to the reader.

options.label: Staleness watermark on every derived item
options.detail: Each derived record carries the newest source seq it covers; the read path reports how many newer source records exist and always lets raw evidence outrank a stale derivation.
options.note: Honest and cheap; the reader still sees old derivations.

options.label: Maximum lag bound
options.detail: The trigger policy guarantees a derived layer is at most T minutes or N deposits behind; breaching it is an alert.
options.note: Operational SLO; needs the trigger policy and backlog metrics.

options.label: Read-your-writes via on-demand refresh
options.detail: A read that hits a dirty derived item refreshes it synchronously (or falls back to raw evidence) before answering.
options.note: Fresh answers but breaks the zero-LLM hot path.

why: Watermarks are the minimum needed for RV04 and RV07 (stale publication after forget, cache identity) and let the read side prefer raw turns over stale summaries; C is an add-on once O-02 C triggers exist. D conflicts with the zero-LLM read decision.

title: Call 2 shape at session close
question: When a session closes, should call 2 be one structured call with sections (summary, stitched episode, profile operations), separate calls per artefact, or should session work stay in the sleep cycle?
today: session_close (workers/pipelines.py:3669) only records a session_closed MARKER and returns status stub; consolidate writes the session summary at sleep instead (workers/pipelines.py:435).
others: Honcho: separate summary tasks (short every 20, long every 60 messages) and separate deduction/dream tasks for the card. EverMemOS: profile add/update/delete/none ops per memcell with caps. MemMachine: background profile ingestion with neighbour-aware ADD/DELETE. Combined: incremental summary per user turn, profile per 10 episodes.

options.label: Leave session work in sleep (today)
options.detail: Keep the hook as a marker; consolidate and reflect_profile produce session artefacts later.
options.note: No new code; session artefacts lag until sleep and run as separate passes.

options.label: One structured call with three sections
options.detail: summary (bounded words), episode (stitched from window fragments with cited windows), profile_ops (add/update/delete/none against the current card, observation date, stated vs inferred); each section validated and deposited independently.
options.note: One call reads the session once; a failed section must not lose the others (RV11).

options.label: Separate calls per artefact
options.detail: Summary, episode and profile each get their own prompt and model role at close.
options.note: Prompts stay focused and can use different models; triple the session-level calls.

options.label: Deterministic close, LLM deferred
options.detail: At close, stitch fragments and build an extractive summary with no call; LLM wording and profile ops run in sleep.
used_by: MemSpine consolidate without a summarize role
options.note: Zero-cost close; profile changes still wait for sleep.

why: G-CALL2 proposes exactly this sectioned call and ADR-066 reserves the slot; per-section validation answers RV11. Gate: G-C9-style screen with no loss outside open-domain and a summary spot audit.

title: Session summary update policy
question: How should session summaries be built and kept from drifting: extractive, incremental with periodic full rebuild, rolling short and long summaries, or a hierarchy of summaries?
today: consolidate writes one summary per closed session of 3+ turns (30-minute gap): extractive first sentence per turn capped at 600 chars (CONSOLIDATION_SUMMARY_MAX_CHARS, config/constants.py:175) without a summarize role, else one LLM call; incremental mode folds new turns with summarize@incremental and rebuilds every 8 (SESSION_SUMMARY_REBUILD_EVERY, constants.py:709; _incremental_summary workers/pipelines.py:721); membership drift archives the old summary with an evolve_to chain.
others: Honcho: short summary every 20 messages and long every 60, recursive, with a degenerate-output guard (<35% distinct 4-grams rejected). Combined: incremental per turn with 250-word cap and full rebuild every 20 questions. MemMachine: rolling summary of evicted turns. LightMem: cross-event summaries over time windows marking facts consolidated.

options.label: Extractive only
options.detail: First sentence per turn, no model.
options.note: Cannot drift or hallucinate, but reads poorly and misses what matters.

options.label: Incremental with periodic rebuild (today, opt-in)
options.detail: Fold new turns into the previous summary; full rebuild every N folds; archived history chain.
options.note: Good cost/quality balance; drift bounded by N.

options.label: B plus degenerate-output guard
options.detail: Reject an output that is repetitive, longer than its cap, or loses named entities present in the previous version; keep the old summary and count the rejection.
options.note: Cheap code guard against the most common small-model failure.

options.label: Hierarchical summaries (session, day, period)
options.detail: Session summaries roll up into period summaries that cite their children.
options.note: Helps very long histories; another derived layer to keep fresh.

why: Incremental-with-rebuild is already built (#56); the Honcho guard is a small code check that protects against small-model loops. Hierarchies (D) are deferred until a long-history workload shows the need.

title: Stitched episodes across windows
question: How should window-level episode fragments become session or cross-session episodes: keep fragments, stitch at session close, LLM-merge neighbouring episodes about the same event, or cluster episodes geometrically?
today: Call 1 can emit an episode fragment per window (window mode all, off); _store_episode keeps title and narrative only (workers/windows.py:894); no stitching; fragments compete as raw text when on (G-W1).
others: Nemori: a new episode is LLM-merged into a top-5 neighbour judged the same event (<1 h apart), both originals deleted. EverMemOS: episodes merged into the nearest cluster at cosine 0.65 within 7 days. MIRIX: episodic merge overwrites summary and details. MemMachine: no episode merge.

options.label: Fragments only (today)
options.detail: One fragment per window, no join.
options.note: Events spanning windows are split across fragments.

options.label: Stitch at session close in call 2
options.detail: The session's fragments are joined into one dated third-person narrative citing its windows; fragments archived as parents, never deleted.
options.note: Uses the call 2 slot; does not join an event that continues in a later session.

options.label: B plus cross-session event merge at sleep
options.detail: Episodes about the same event (time, participants, embedding) are merged with lineage; originals kept as history.
options.note: Best for long-running threads; a wrong merge mixes two events unless reversible.

options.label: Geometric clusters, no LLM
options.detail: Assign each episode to the nearest cluster within a time window; clusters feed retrieval and reflection.
options.note: Cheap grouping, no merged narrative.

why: G-CALL2 includes the stitched episode and G-W1 needs an episode retrieval unit; BD-4 (keep history, never overwrite) rules out destructive merges, so C stays a later, reversible option.

title: Reconciling the online deposit backlog
question: When online (call 1) deposits create provisional names and facts without LLM merges, how and when should the background reconcile that backlog: at the next sleep, in a bounded continuous reconciler, or never (aliases only)?
today: With G-W49 planned, new names are resolved in code with llm=None and marked pending_merge for sleep; today edges wait in an in-memory buffer for extract_graph and the resolver runs only at sleep (workers/pipelines.py:1983); RV01 found take_edges clears before acknowledgement.
others: Honcho: a reconciler task type hard-deletes soft-deleted rows and fixes up vectors. Hindsight: a 300 s reconcile loop beside per-retain consolidation. Graphiti / Combined: resolution inline per episode, so no backlog. Mnemon: background jobs merge the ledger after a watermark.

options.label: Resolve everything at sleep (today's model)
options.detail: Pending items wait for the next cycle; the whole backlog is processed then.
options.note: Duplicate entities are visible to reads until the next sleep.

options.label: Persisted backlog with age and size caps
options.detail: Pending merges are persisted items; the trigger policy fires call 3 when the backlog exceeds a size or age cap; items are acknowledged only after the merge commits.
options.note: Bounded duplicate window; survives restart (RV01).

options.label: Resolve inline with LLM per write
options.detail: No backlog: each new name and fact is adjudicated before it is stored.
options.note: Clean graph immediately; 13-49x hot-path call cost (RV10).

options.label: Never merge, alias edges only
options.detail: Keep provisional entities separate and link them with soft alias edges the reader can follow.
options.note: Never a wrong merge, but entity-centric reads fragment.

why: RV01 requires derived work to survive restart and be acknowledged after commit; G-W49 deliberately defers LLM merges to sleep, so the backlog needs explicit caps rather than an unbounded wait.

title: Entity resolution and LLM confirmation
question: How far should background entity resolution go: deterministic rules only, rules then LLM for the unresolved, LLM confirmation of every proposed merge, or scoped resolution that also uses type and context?
today: EntityResolver ladder (memories/associative/resolution.py): exact, alias table, top-15 embedding candidates, entropy gate, MinHash Jaccard 0.9, then (resolve: llm only) one resolve_entity@batch call per 50 names; trust guard 0.2 records contested instead of merging (config/constants.py:460-481).
others: Graphiti / Combined: exact name, MinHash (Jaccard >= 0.9) with entropy gate, then LLM dedupe for the rest. Hindsight: rule-based only, pg_trgm 0.3 plus co-occurrence, no LLM. Mem0: exact text or top-1 cosine >= 0.95. Cognee: deterministic name ids, fuzzy merge 0.85 as an explicit pipeline.

options.label: Rules only
options.detail: Exact, alias, MinHash; ambiguous short names stay separate.
options.note: No call, no wrong LLM merge; misses nicknames like Bram / Abraham.

options.label: Rules then LLM for unresolved (today, opt-in)
options.detail: Only names the ladder cannot settle go to a batched LLM call with candidates.
options.note: Few calls; the LLM still sees names without context.

options.label: B with type and context, ambiguity preserved
options.detail: Candidates scoped by entity type and co-mentioned entities; the LLM sees one evidence line per side; a low-confidence answer keeps both entities linked as possible-same instead of merging.
options.note: Handles homonyms (two people called Ilse); thresholds must be calibrated per mechanism (RV17).

options.label: LLM confirms every merge
options.detail: Even MinHash hits are confirmed by the model.
options.note: Highest precision, cost grows with every alias.

why: RV17 confirms the same name can be different entities and that MinHash and cosine thresholds are separate mechanisms; keeping ambiguity explicit fits BD-4 (no destructive overwrite) and the trust guard already records contested merges.

title: Cross-key contradiction and invalidation
question: Beyond the same-key conflict ladder, how should the background find and settle facts that contradict each other under different keys?
today: Deterministic 13-rung conflict ladder for same-key facts (supersede / contest / backfill); G-2 cross-key check _retract_contradicted (workers/pipelines.py:1902) is opt-in (extract_graph contradictions, pipelines.py:2023): up to 3 same-subject candidates ranked by shared words (CONTRADICTION_CANDIDATES, constants.py:869) go to invalidate_edge; update/invalidate retracts the old key through the semantic door (valid_to set, history kept).
others: Graphiti / Combined: resolve_edge returns duplicate and contradicted facts; code sets invalid_at and expired_at. Hindsight: consolidation LLM per batch of 8 new facts updates or deletes related observations. Cognee (opt-in): detect_contradictions adds a non-destructive contradicts edge. LightMem / Honcho / MemMachine: LLM deletes the older value.

options.label: Same-key ladder only
options.detail: Facts under different keys never invalidate each other.
options.note: Misses 'moved to Ghent' versus 'lives in Utrecht' stored under different attributes.

options.label: Word-overlap candidates, LLM adjudication (today, opt-in)
options.detail: Top 3 same-subject live facts by shared words, one verdict each; retraction closes validity.
options.note: Cheap; candidate recall depends on shared words.

options.label: Subject + predicate family + time + embedding candidates
options.detail: Candidates from the same subject and predicate family or embedding neighbours within the validity window; batched verdicts; result can be supersede, contest (kept open), or coexist.
options.note: Better recall (RV17); cost bounded by batching and the O-05 budget.

options.label: Flag only, never invalidate
options.detail: Add a contradicts link and let the reader decide.
options.note: Safest against wrong invalidation; pushes the work to every read.

why: RV17 says contradiction search must use subject, predicate and time, not only similarity; the G0 integration split (supersede / contest / coexist) and BD-4 history mean a wrong verdict is reversible, which makes better recall worth the extra adjudications.

title: Near-duplicate consolidation and reinforcement
question: How should repeated or near-duplicate facts be consolidated offline: exact dedupe only, cosine merge with a reinforcement count, LLM merge adjudication above a threshold, or no merge with grouping deferred to observations?
today: Semantic write merges at cosine 0.92 (DEDUP_COSINE_THRESHOLD, config/constants.py:55) and bumps importance by 0.1 and utility; records keep corroborations; scoring weights for importance are 0 in base (ADR-030), so reinforcement does not affect ranking (G-W40).
others: Honcho: exact plus cosine distance <= 0.05, richer text wins, times_derived bumped. Hindsight: observation at cosine >= 0.97 against top 5 triggers an LLM merge/keep call. LightMem: offline LLM update/delete/ignore for neighbours above 0.9. Memori: exact sha256, num_times incremented.

options.label: Exact dedupe only
options.detail: Normalised text hash; repeats counted.
options.note: Paraphrased repeats pile up and crowd the context.

options.label: Cosine merge plus reinforcement count (today, refined)
options.detail: Merge above a calibrated threshold, keep the richer text, count repeats as reinforcement with a bounded ranking boost that never overrides relevance.
options.note: Cheap; a fixed threshold can merge two different numeric facts.

options.label: LLM merge adjudication in a narrow band
options.detail: Above a high threshold merge directly, in a grey band ask the model merge / keep both, below keep both; qualifiers (numbers, dates, negation) block merges.
options.note: Fewer wrong merges; one call per grey-band pair.

options.label: Never merge facts; group into observations
options.detail: Facts stay append-only; duplicates are absorbed by the observation layer (O-15).
options.note: Full provenance, but the fact store keeps growing.

why: Already built and cheap; G-W40 adds the bounded reinforcement boost (off by default, Hindsight-style) and RV17 demands calibration per embedding model. Add C's qualifier guard (numbers, dates, negation) as code, not an LLM call.

title: Value histories for keyed state
question: Should keyed state (where someone lives, a job title, a preference) be exposed as an explicit value history per subject and attribute, and if so built deterministically or by the model?
today: The conflict ladder supersedes and contests per key and records keep validity intervals and history, readable with as-of reads; there is no consolidated per-key history view (G-W29 'missing').
others: Mnemon: consolidation appends a dated value under the same key and sets conflict=true on contradiction. Hindsight: observations carry history and proof counts. MemMachine / MIRIX / LightMem: overwrite or delete, no history. Graphiti: invalid_at chains per edge.

options.label: Implicit history in records (today)
options.detail: History exists as superseded records; the reader assembles it.
options.note: Correct but the reader may get only the latest or a random older value.

options.label: Deterministic history view per (subject, attribute)
options.detail: Code builds one view per key: values in effective-time order with source dates, current value, open contests; no LLM.
options.note: Answers 'what was it before' directly; depends on good keys (G-W50).

options.label: LLM-written history narrative
options.detail: The model writes 'moved from Utrecht to Ghent in 2024' per changed key.
options.note: Readable, but an inference stored as memory unless every step cites its source.

options.label: Overwrite latest only
options.detail: Keep the current value, discard history.
options.note: Rejected by BD-4: loses auditability and as-of answers.

why: G-W29 proposes grouping by (subject, attribute) with history; doing it in code keeps 'never store an inference as a fact' and RV04 needs effective-time semantics separate from observation history.

title: Observation layer (consolidated beliefs)
question: Should the engine maintain a layer of consolidated observations over many facts (with proof counts and citations), and should groups be formed by code with the LLM only rewriting changed groups, or fully by the LLM?
today: Not present; mine_facts and predict_calibrate are sleep-time fact miners (workers/schedule.py:59-71), and reflections (reflective memory) exist but are per-session insights, not a maintained belief set.
others: Hindsight: consolidation LLM per batch of up to 8 new facts emits create/update/delete over related observations (one per facet, cascade state changes), with proof counts and staleness. LightMem: StructMem cross-event summaries over time windows with covered fact ids. Honcho: deductive and inductive conclusions written by the dreamer. MemOS: cluster summary parents under reorganise.

options.label: No observation layer (today)
options.detail: Readers combine raw facts at answer time.
options.note: Context fills with many small overlapping facts.

options.label: Code-grouped, LLM-worded for changed groups
options.detail: Group facts by key and by embedding neighbourhood; one observation per group with history, proof count and cited parents; only groups whose membership changed reach the LLM.
options.note: Fewer context tokens with provenance; group thresholds need calibration.

options.label: LLM-managed observation set
options.detail: The model sees new facts plus related observations and returns create/update/delete operations.
options.note: Flexible grouping; drift and inference creep unless ops are validated against citations.

options.label: Cluster summaries only
options.detail: Summaries per topic cluster, no per-belief objects.
options.note: Coarser; already partly covered by communities (O-17).

why: G-W29's proposal: deterministic grouping with only changed groups sent to the LLM; gate is MAB-CR blind with context tokens down and no loss. Observations must stay derived (trust capped at the minimum of parents, G1) so taint and forget cascade.

title: Entity summaries
question: How should per-entity summaries be produced and refreshed: off, at sleep with a no-call fast path and batched LLM (today), on every write touching the entity, or built lazily at read?
today: summarize_entities (workers/pipelines.py:2621, off, needs the graph): entities whose dated lines fit 2,000 chars get a no-call summary; longer ones go to summarize_entity in batches of 30 (ENTITY_SUMMARY_BATCH, constants.py:440); a membership watermark skips unchanged entities; trust = minimum of members.
others: Graphiti / Combined: refreshed per episode from new edges only, LLM skipped under 2,000 chars, batches of 30. Hindsight: entity observation network removed, 'summaries now live in mental models'. MIRIX: semantic entries about people stand in. Honcho: peer card per observed peer instead.

options.label: Off
options.detail: No entity summaries; entity reads use facts.
options.note: Entity-centric questions need many fact hits.

options.label: Sleep-time with fast path (today, opt-in)
options.detail: Summaries rebuilt at sleep for changed entities only.
options.note: Cheap and incremental; stale between sleeps.

options.label: Refresh per write
options.detail: Each deposit touching an entity updates its summary.
options.note: Fresh but on the write path.

options.label: Profile-style card per important entity
options.detail: Only entities above a mention threshold get a capped, typed card (identity, attributes, relations) instead of free text.
options.note: Bounded size and schema; needs the card schema from O-19.

why: Already built with the Graphiti fast path and watermark; keeping it at sleep preserves the zero-LLM write path (G-W49 rationale). Revisit D once the profile card schema exists.

title: Communities and reorganisation
question: Should the background build topic groupings over memory, and with which method: none, graph community detection with summary parents (today), embedding clusters, or topic threads?
today: reorganize (workers/pipelines.py:1176, off unless the graph and [community] extra): Leiden plus 10 LPA refinement passes or LPA alone with a collapse guard (share > 0.5 rejected at >= 100 nodes); communities of >= 3 get a summary parent; refresh when changes exceed 10% or every 5 sleeps (config/constants.py:94-119); read.graph_communities off.
others: Graphiti / Combined: label propagation, 24 h cooldown, off by default and never formatted into context. MemOS: recursive MiniBatchKMeans clusters (<= 20), LLM summary parents (off by default). EverMemOS: geometry clusters at cosine 0.65 in 7 days. Mnemon: topic threads assigned by the fold model.

options.label: No groupings
options.detail: Drop the reorganize stage.
options.note: Most engines run without them; nothing in scope reads them today.

options.label: Graph communities with summary parents (today)
options.detail: Keep Leiden/LPA, guards and incremental refresh; off by default.
options.note: Built; value unproven because no read path uses it.

options.label: Embedding clusters over facts and episodes
options.detail: Cluster by vectors (no graph needed), summary parent per cluster.
options.note: Works without a graph; clusters drift as embeddings change.

options.label: Topic threads
options.detail: Each event is assigned to one named sub-topic thread at consolidation.
options.note: Readable structure for agents; one more LLM assignment per event.

why: Keep the built stage off by default and do not invest further until a read leg consumes it (survey: Graphiti also builds communities nobody reads). Gate any use on a global-question workload.

title: How the profile is updated
question: How should the user profile be maintained: caller-set only, free reflections, guarded add/update/delete/none operations against the current card, or periodic full rebuilds?
today: The persona is caller-set (set_persona) and pinned; reflect_profile (workers/pipelines.py:3484, off) writes per-session insights into reflective memory with evidence ids; profile_header_packing (off) packs summaries, insights and hits under a PROFILE NOTES header (PROFILE_HEADER_TOP_K = 8).
others: EverMemOS: add/update/delete/none ops under a per-owner lock; an older observation cannot overwrite a newer item. MemMachine: LLM DELETE then ADD per feature, consolidation once 20+ features. Combined: full build at 10 user episodes, rebuild every 10, incremental between. Honcho: only the dreamer writes the card via update_peer_card.

options.label: Caller-set persona plus free reflections (today)
options.detail: No maintained card; insights accumulate as reflective records.
options.note: Insights pile up and can contradict each other.

options.label: Guarded operations against a card
options.detail: Call 2 proposes add/update/delete/none per item with observation date and stated vs inferred; code applies ops only if newer, cited and within caps; deletes become supersedes with history.
options.note: Bounded, auditable card; ops can be wrong, so guards matter.

options.label: Periodic full rebuild
options.detail: Rebuild the card from recent sessions every N sessions.
options.note: Self-corrects drift but forgets older stable traits outside the window.

options.label: B plus periodic rebuild check
options.detail: Ops between rebuilds; a rebuild every N sessions is diffed against the card and differences reconciled as ops.
options.note: Best drift control; most moving parts.

why: G-CALL2 specifies profile_ops against the current card with stated vs inferred; BD-4 means deletions become supersedes. A rebuild check (D) can follow if audits show drift.

title: Profile card schema, caps and inferences
question: What shape should the profile card take: free text, a typed card with code-enforced caps, per-category caps, or an agent-edited block, and may it contain inferred traits?
today: No card schema or caps (G-W30 built-off); PROFILE_PACK_MAX_SHARE = 0.5 caps the packed header share (config/constants.py:705); relevance gating of the profile header exists.
others: Honcho: four prefixes (IDENTITY / ATTRIBUTE / RELATIONSHIP / INSTRUCTION), 200 chars per entry, 40 entries, enforced in code. EverMemOS: explicit_info and implicit_traits, 60 items, 8 per category. MIRIX: human and persona core blocks, 5,000 chars each, always injected whole. Mnemon: directives only (stated instructions and preferences), 1,500-char budget.

options.label: Free text, uncapped (today's packing)
options.detail: Whatever reflections and summaries the packer selects.
options.note: Unbounded and leaks into unrelated answers (OP-Bench lesson).

options.label: Typed card, code caps, stated-only by default
options.detail: identity / attribute / relationship / instruction entries, per-entry and total caps, each entry cited and marked stated; inferred entries off unless enabled; injected only when relevant.
options.note: Small, safe, auditable; inferred traits need an explicit opt-in.

options.label: Per-category caps with implicit traits
options.detail: Categories with per-category limits and an implicit-traits section.
options.note: Richer personalisation; inferred traits risk becoming facts.

options.label: Agent-edited core block
options.detail: The agent appends and rewrites a capped text block that is always injected.
options.note: Flexible; always-on injection and model-written content.

why: G-W30 proposes the typed card with code caps, stated-only default and relevance-gated injection; gate: OP-Bench irrelevance not worse and hand-audit precision >= 90%. Matches the rule 'never store an inference as a fact'.

title: Reflection and insight generation
question: When and over what should reflections (higher-level insights) be generated: off, once per consolidated session (today), when accumulated importance crosses a threshold, or periodically over clusters?
today: reflect_profile (off) writes insights per consolidated session once (done marker); each reflection names its evidence records, inherits taint and is depth-capped at 2 (REFLECTION_DEPTH_CAP, config/constants.py:122; memories/reflective/reflections.py).
others: Generative Agents: reflect when summed importance of recent events crosses a threshold. EverMemOS: opt-in weekly reflection merges a cluster keeping the latest state. Honcho: inductive conclusions from the dream specialist. Cognee: distill_sessions packs a session into lessons with a writer / rejecter pair.

options.label: Off
options.detail: No reflective layer.
options.note: No derived inferences to go wrong.

options.label: Per session, cited, depth-capped (today, opt-in)
options.detail: One reflection call per closed session; insights carry evidence ids and trust caps.
options.note: Predictable cost; insights repeat across sessions with no merge.

options.label: Threshold-triggered over recent memory
options.detail: Reflect when accumulated importance or new-fact count crosses a threshold, over a window spanning sessions; new insights merged with existing ones.
options.note: Cross-session insight; needs an importance signal (G-P7) and merge.

options.label: Writer plus rejecter pair
options.detail: A second check accepts an insight only if it is supported by cited evidence and not already known.
options.note: Higher precision at double cost.

why: Reflections are inferences: keep the cited, depth-capped design, off by default, and feed accepted insights into the profile ops path (O-18) rather than injecting them separately. Revisit C once G-P7 importance labels exist.

title: Standing answers (mental models)
question: Should the engine maintain answers to standing questions (for example 'what are Ilse's dietary preferences') that are refreshed in the background and read with no retrieval?
today: Not present (G-W39 missing).
others: Hindsight: user-defined mental models refreshed after consolidation by edit operations so untouched sections stay byte-identical; read is a DB read with no LLM call. Honcho: the peer card plus a 'representation' selection of conclusions. MIRIX: always-injected core blocks.

options.label: None (today)
options.detail: Every question goes through retrieval.
options.note: No stale precomputed answers.

options.label: Opt-in standing questions with delta refresh
options.detail: Per-namespace questions registered by the host; refreshed when a cited source changes, by section edits; citations pruned when parents are forgotten.
options.note: Fast stable answers; staleness and forget cascade must be handled.

options.label: Full regeneration each cycle
options.detail: Recompute every standing answer at each sleep.
options.note: Simple but expensive and churns text.

options.label: Cache of recent answers
options.detail: Cache read results for repeated questions, invalidated by watermark.
options.note: No new memory type; only helps exact repeats.

why: G-W39 marks this a product feature for wave D: opt-in, delta refresh and pruned citations; it relies on O-06 watermarks and the forget cascade (RV07).

title: Decay, forgetting and compression
question: What should the background do with old or unused memory: nothing, move it down access tiers and compress it (today), score it by importance and recency for eviction, summarise-and-archive it, or enforce per-type caps?
today: decay_sweep (workers/pipelines.py:868) moves idle records hot to warm 7 d, warm to cold 30 d, cold to dormant 90 d (config/constants.py:131-133), access restores hot; compress (pipelines.py:921) zstd-encodes cold-tier content (meaning unchanged, legal hold respected); nothing is deleted except by retention classes or forget.
others: Hindsight / Honcho / EverMemOS / Mnemon: no decay; recency only as a ranking boost. MemOS: FIFO hard delete under per-type caps. Cognee: preference weights decay on read; EMA feedback. MIRIX: raw task memories deleted after 14 days by an operator job. Combined: optional archival of transcripts older than 30 days, revived on read.

options.label: No decay
options.detail: Keep everything at one tier; recency only in ranking.
options.note: Simplest; storage and index grow without bound.

options.label: Access tiers plus cold compression (today)
options.detail: Idle tiers, zstd at rest, no semantic loss, reinforcement by access.
options.note: Never loses meaning; tiers do not yet change ranking or index membership.

options.label: Importance x recency score with eviction
options.detail: Ebbinghaus-style strength from importance, reinforcement and age; below a floor, records leave the hot index.
options.note: Can forget a rarely mentioned but crucial fact (allergy).

options.label: Summarise-and-archive cold episodes
options.detail: Cold sessions are represented by their summary in the hot index; raw turns kept in cold storage and revived on demand.
options.note: Smaller hot index; recall of cold detail needs a revive path.

options.label: Per-type caps, FIFO
options.detail: Hard limits per memory type; oldest deleted.
options.note: Predictable size, silent loss.

why: Most surveyed engines found no benefit from destructive forgetting and BD-4 values history; keep the lossless tiers and add D only when hot-index size becomes a measured cost. Pinned facts (stated instructions, safety-relevant attributes) must be exempt from any future eviction.

title: Prospective memory and foresight
question: What forward-looking memory should the background create: watches from stated plans only (today), anticipated questions as retrieval cues, model-predicted future states, or push delivery of due items?
today: Prospective watches from stated plans (auto_watch), pull-based via Engine.due(); check_watches (workers/pipelines.py:977) only logs fired counts; anticipate (pipelines.py:3446, off) stores likely future questions as cues on the answering turns, firewall-screened and never assembled as content (H8).
others: EverMemOS: up to 10 foresight predictions per cell, now off by default because nothing reads them. MIRIX: no prospective layer. Honcho / Hindsight: none. memU: host agent scheduler can act on reminders.

options.label: Stated plans only, pull delivery (today)
options.detail: Watches only from explicit user plans; host polls due().
options.note: Never stores speculation; host must poll.

options.label: A plus anticipated-question cues
options.detail: Background writes likely future questions as retrieval keys on the turns that answer them (never as content).
options.note: Improves recall for indirect phrasing; one call per session.

options.label: Model-predicted future states
options.detail: Store predictions ('Bram will likely change jobs') as memory with expiry.
options.note: Speculation stored as memory; rejected by BD-6.

options.label: A plus push delivery
options.detail: Fired watches are pushed to subscribers (webhook / event) during the background cycle.
options.note: Useful for agents; delivery guarantees become a new contract.

why: BD-6 keeps plans from stated text only; cues are retrieval keys, not facts, so they respect that rule. Push delivery (D) is a protocol decision that can follow later.

title: Procedural memory: skills and lessons
question: How should procedural memory be learned offline: fixed-template lessons from outcome receipts (today), slot-filled procedure cases from trajectories, model-written skills with staged promotion, or host-agent-written skill files?
today: Lessons from structured outcome receipts rendered by a fixed template, advisory only, never executable (memories/procedural/lessons.py, ADR-060); skills carry a stage ladder (SkillStage.ADVISORY / STAGED) with trust caps.
others: MIRIX: budgeted skill evolution every 5 sealed task sessions. MemOS: skill crystallisation. memU: skill files written by the host agent ('self-evolve'). Cognee: distill_sessions lessons accepted by a writer / rejecter pair. LightMem FluxMem: skills induced per KMeans cluster.

options.label: Template lessons from receipts (today)
options.detail: Caller supplies task, action, outcome, reason; engine fills a fixed template.
options.note: Cannot be injected or drift; learns only what the host reports.

options.label: Slot-filled procedure cases from trajectories
options.detail: The background extracts steps, preconditions and outcome into fixed slots from agent trajectories; rendered by template, advisory stage only.
options.note: Learns from traces without free model text; needs trajectory capture.

options.label: Model-written skills, staged promotion
options.detail: The model writes a skill; it moves advisory to staged to executable after evidence of success.
options.note: Most capable; a model-written skill is an injection and drift vector (BD-2).

options.label: Host-agent-written skill files
options.detail: The engine stores and retrieves skill files the host agent edits.
options.note: Pushes responsibility to the host; engine cannot vouch for content.

why: BD-2 rejects free model-written skills as an injection vector and proposes slot-filled cases rendered by template at advisory stage only, when agent trajectories are in scope.

title: Implicit feedback from conversation
question: Should the background infer feedback on served memories from the conversation itself (corrections, thanks, repeats), and with what judge: none, rules, a local classifier, or an LLM rater?
today: Explicit feedback verb only (like / dislike / note); lessons count likes, dislikes and access (lessons.py docstring); no implicit signal (G-W47 missing).
others: Cognee: rates the previous answer and served context each turn with an LLM and moves feedback_weight by EMA (alpha 0.1). Honcho: none. MemOS: usage history recorded on retrieval but unused. Hindsight: none since the opinion confidence was removed.

options.label: Explicit feedback only (today)
options.detail: Only caller-sent like/dislike/note.
options.note: No self-reinforcement risk; little signal in practice.

options.label: Rule-detected corrections at sleep
options.detail: Patterns such as 'no, I said', 'that's wrong', or a repeated question after an answer flag the served records for review (not reweighting).
options.note: Cheap; language-specific and low recall.

options.label: Local classifier via the decision port
options.detail: A small local model scores each answer turn; signals adjust a bounded utility score with EMA, never relevance.
options.note: G-W47's revisit path; needs labelled data.

options.label: LLM rater per turn
options.detail: An LLM rates the previous answer and served context; weights move by EMA.
options.note: Extra call per turn and self-reinforcement risk.

why: G-W47 defers this: an LLM rater costs a call per turn and risks self-reinforcement; revisit with a local classifier (C) once the decision port and labelled data exist.

title: Per-observer views (theory of mind)
question: In multi-party or multi-agent settings, should the background build separate derived views of what each observer knows or believes about each subject, or keep one shared view with perspective tags?
today: Perspective tags on every turn (speaker, addressee, subject, asker, modality, reported speech; core/perspective.py), one store per namespace; derived layers are not split by observer (G-W48 partial).
others: Honcho: one collection per (observer, observed) pair; one extraction fanned out to every observer; a peer card per pair. MIRIX: per-agent memory managers but one user view. Mnemon / Hindsight: one view per bank or scope.

options.label: One view plus tags (today)
options.detail: Read-side filters on perspective tags answer 'what did Bram tell Ilse'.
options.note: Enough for single-user assistants; no 'as seen by' summaries.

options.label: Derived 'about X as seen by Y' views at sleep
options.detail: Built from perspective tags for the multi-agent template only: per pair, the facts Y heard or stated about X, with a capped card.
options.note: Theory-of-mind answers; cost scales with observer pairs.

options.label: Per-pair collections at write
options.detail: Each deposit is fanned out into every observer's collection.
options.note: Fully separated beliefs; storage and extraction multiply.

why: G-W48 proposes derived per-observer views at sleep for the multi-agent template only, reusing existing tags; the single-user default stays unchanged.

title: Read tiers and who chooses depth
question: Should v2 expose read depth as a per-call level (cheap zero-LLM vs deep model-assisted), and who picks it: the caller, a router, or configuration?
today: Zero-LLM read is the default; agentic loop, slot loop, read-time fact chain and event ledger are config switches (read.agentic, read.agentic_mode, read.fact_chain, read.event_ledger in config/schema.py:1154-1222), not a per-call argument (G-W41 partial).
others: Honcho: get_context (0 LLM) vs dialectic chat with caller-chosen reasoning_level minimal..max (1-11 calls). Hindsight: recall (0 LLM, budget low/mid/high sets arm depth 100/300/1000) vs reflect agent (up to 10 iterations). MemOS: fast (default) vs fine mode per request. MemMachine: agent_mode flag per deployment.

options.label: Config switches only (today)
options.detail: One read path per deployment; enhancers toggled in YAML.
options.note: Simple, but one agent cannot ask for a deeper read on a hard question.

options.label: Per-call depth: fast / standard / deep
options.detail: A 'depth' argument maps to existing enhancers with fixed call and token caps; default fast = zero-LLM.
options.note: Caller pays only when it asks; needs per-tier budgets and tests.

options.label: Per-call depth plus auto escalation
options.detail: As B, and a cheap signal (contract unsure, gate weak, multi-hop shape) may lift fast to standard within a cap.
options.note: Hidden cost variance; escalation trigger must be screened.

options.label: Always deep (LLM decider each read)
options.detail: Every read runs a judge or tool loop over candidates.
options.note: Kept out by design (BD-1); 8x cost observed for no gain.

why: The field pattern is a zero-LLM hot read with an opt-in deep tier; our only deep-tier screen (E02 slot loop) was net -3 at about 8x wall time (RV12), so depth must be a caller decision with caps, not a default (G-W41, BD-1).

title: Default unit of evidence returned
question: What is the default evidence unit a read returns: raw turns with neighbour windows, derived facts, or a mixed bundle of raw plus capped derived notes?
today: Base template pins read.default_mode: replay (config/templates/base.yaml:19; schema default auto, config/schema.py:427): one ranked list of raw turns expanded into neighbour windows, chronological; derived layers are mostly off the read path.
others: Mem0: facts only, caller formats. EverMemOS: episodes with nested facts. Mnemon: one View coarse-to-fine (instructions, topic timelines, value histories, then raw records). MemMachine: short-term episodes + summary, long-term windows, profile features side by side.

options.label: Raw windows only (today)
options.detail: Raw turns are authoritative; derived layers only route.
options.note: Faithful and grounded, but long contexts and no aggregation.

options.label: Facts only
options.detail: Return extracted assertions with dates.
options.note: Compact but extraction loss becomes answer loss.

options.label: Mixed bundle: raw evidence first, derived as capped notes
options.detail: Raw windows hold most of the budget; facts, summaries, profile and timelines enter as labelled notes under per-block caps, each pointing to its source.
options.note: Best of both if packing and lifting are right (R-17, R-18).

options.label: Typed sections per memory type
options.detail: Each memory type returned as its own section with its own top-k, no cross-type ranking.
options.note: Readable, but no global budget and no one score.

why: Raw truth stays authoritative (RV09: preserve direct evidence) while derived layers become usable on the read path, which is the precondition for G-W8 and G-W25; the review proposes exactly this 'one evidence-aware token budget'.

title: Typed query contract adoption
question: Should the typed query contract (subjects, relation, answer type, time scope, cardinality, request kind) become the default query analysis, and in which form?
today: read.query_contract: off (config/schema.py:970; core/query_contract.py:86); heuristic and llm (one plan@contract call only when rules are unsure) are opt-in; used as a reader header and reranker hint. Focus screen f-contract-i2: net +9 (+15/-6) at equal calls and tokens; full run and blind sets pending (A03 CANDIDATE).
others: Hindsight: non-LLM dateparser analyser for a time window only. Mnemon: parallel need-plan call (NEED/ALL). MemOS fine mode: LLM goal parser (keys, tags, intent). Mem0 and Memori: lemmas and length only.

options.label: Off (today)
options.detail: Only rule-based question shape (ordering, set).
options.note: Loses a measured +9 candidate gain.

options.label: Heuristic contract on by default
options.detail: Rules fill the contract; it feeds header, rerank hint and routing; zero model calls.
options.note: Free; rules are language-dependent.

options.label: Heuristic plus LLM fallback when unsure
options.detail: As B; one small call only when the rules are not confident about type or scope.
options.note: Better on other languages and odd phrasings; tail latency.

options.label: LLM planner every read
options.detail: Model writes the contract, needs and sub-queries each time.
options.note: Moves the read into the deep tier.

why: A03 measured net +9 with no extra calls or tokens; adopt the zero-call form as default only after the full run and the blind sets (MAB-CR, ConvoMem) confirm no category loss beyond its band (G-E1), keep C as the multilingual option.

title: Routing and query rewriting
question: How should the read route a question to legs, modes and probes: fixed pipeline, rule router from the contract, or a model planner with rewrites?
today: Rules planner exists (read.planner: rules|decision|llm, config/schema.py:503) but only routes under mode=auto, which the base template bypasses with replay; rule probes (pseudo-relevance feedback, multi-intent, bridge hop, cluster expand) and LLM subqueries are opt-in (engine.py:6064-6171).
others: Cognee: rule router (absolute-date questions to TEMPORAL, else hybrid). MemMachine agent mode: one ToolSelect LLM call to SplitQuery / ChainOfQuery / direct. Combined: history-aware reformulation plus planner writing 2-3 third-person queries. Mnemon: planner writes record-worded searches plus a HyDE note.

options.label: Fixed pipeline (today in practice)
options.detail: Same legs for every question; shape flags tweak list and order.
options.note: Predictable; ignores what the question needs.

options.label: Contract-driven rule router
options.detail: The typed contract switches legs and weights (time scope to temporal leg, many-cardinality to list mode, named subject to entity leg), zero calls.
used_by: Hindsight (temporal arm only when a window is found)
options.note: Every route needs a screen; misroutes are silent.

options.label: LLM rewrite / multi-query
options.detail: Model rewrites into 2-3 stored-record-style queries (optionally HyDE), fused.
options.note: Helps vague questions; adds a call to every read.

options.label: Router in deep tier only
options.detail: B by default; C available only when the caller asks for depth deep.
options.note: Keeps the hot path free; two code paths.

why: Rewrites are the field's deep-tier tool and cost a call per read; a zero-call router driven by the A03 contract captures the cheap part, consistent with the tier split in R-01 and the by-design rejection of an always-on decider (BD-1).

title: Default retrieval leg set
question: Which retrieval legs should run by default in v2, and which stay as screened opt-ins?
today: Engine default vector + BM25 + temporal (base template), perspective leg default True (config/schema.py:919); 22 further leg kinds built and off: entity, graph, session, sentence, recency, view tags, maxsim, word vector, bridge, cluster expand, person-time and others (engine.py:5390-5452, 2397-2504).
others: Hindsight: four arms per fact type in parallel (semantic, keyword, graph, temporal). Mem0: dense + keyword + entity, but only dense candidates scored. Memori: one dense leg with BM25 re-score. MemOS: working, long-term, user, tool, skill, preference legs in parallel.

options.label: Vector + BM25 + temporal + perspective (today)
options.detail: Small default, everything else opt-in.
options.note: Proven; graph and entity layers never reach users.

options.label: Minimal: vector + lexical
options.detail: Two legs, everything else via router or tiers.
options.note: Loses date questions that need a window leg.

options.label: Four-arm default (vector, lexical, temporal, graph/entity)
options.detail: Hindsight-style: each arm bounded, graph one hop from semantic seeds.
options.note: Needs the graph layer to be fresh at read time (G-W49).

options.label: Core three plus router-activated legs
options.detail: Vector, lexical, temporal always; entity, graph, episode, session legs switched on per question by the contract router.
options.note: Leg cost only where it helps; depends on router quality.

why: Running every built leg dilutes RRF with correlated votes (I75: the perspective leg replays the vector order); routing extra legs from the contract keeps cost flat, and each leg still must pass its own focus and blind screen (G-W6, G-W1, G-E1).

title: Lexical leg: BM25 vs learned sparse
question: What should the lexical leg be: classic BM25, a learned sparse model, a static word-vector leg, or BM25 with a word-vector companion?
today: BM25 leg on by default (index.lexical); word_vector_leg (model2vec or word2vec, config/schema.py:860-866) built and off; no learned sparse (SPLADE-style) encoder in src; LadybugDB FTS verified as a backend option (ADR-064).
others: Mem0: fastembed Qdrant/bm25 sparse vector on Qdrant. Hindsight: Postgres tsvector by default, pluggable real BM25 (vchord_bm25, ParadeDB) and CJK tokenisers. Mnemon: in-process BM25 with CJK bigrams and literal codes. Memori: BM25 only over the dense pool, ASCII tokeniser (non-Latin gets nothing).

options.label: BM25 (today)
