options.detail: Okapi BM25 over the full store as an independent leg.
options.note: Strong on names and rare tokens; weak on paraphrase.

options.label: Learned sparse (SPLADE-type)
options.detail: Replace BM25 with expansion-aware sparse vectors.
options.note: Model-dependent, mostly English; extra encoder at write and read.

options.label: BM25 plus word-vector leg
options.detail: Keep BM25; add a cheap static-embedding leg for near-synonyms.
options.note: Correlates with the dense leg; needs the protected pool.

options.label: BM25 with language-aware tokenisers
options.detail: Pluggable tokeniser per namespace language (CJK bigrams, stemming), literal codes kept.
options.note: Generic gain for non-English users; no model cost.

why: BM25 is the leg whose gold is lost in fusion cuts (I75), so it stays independent; the generic weakness across engines is tokenisation for non-Latin text (Memori, Mem0), while the word-vector leg showed only a small set-recall lift and learned sparse has no evidence here.

title: Temporal leg and relative-time anchoring
question: How should the temporal leg resolve time scope: absolute dates only, relative phrases against the read clock, or relative phrases against the question's anchor date with a ranked window?
today: Temporal leg fires on absolute date spans only (config/schema.py:363-385, engine.py:2430-2462); temporal_relative is opt-in and resolves against the read clock, not the question's anchor (G-W33 partial); earlier screen B4 showed no gain on one dataset.
others: Hindsight: dateparser window relative to query_timestamp, candidates inside the window ranked by semantic relevance, proximity boost at rerank. MIRIX: rule parser relative to wall-clock now (wrong for history). Cognee: one LLM call extracts an interval, rerank by overlap. Combined: planner resolves against wall clock, unused.

options.label: Absolute dates only (today)
options.detail: Relative phrases ignored by the leg.
options.note: Misses 'last week' style questions everywhere.

options.label: Rule window anchored to the question time
options.detail: Resolve relative phrases against the caller's reference time (default now), rank by similarity inside the window, coarse precision kept as spans.
options.note: Zero calls; rule coverage per language.

options.label: LLM interval extraction
options.detail: One call turns the time phrase into an interval.
options.note: Handles odd phrasing; a call per dated question.

options.label: B plus event-time index
options.detail: Window matches event intervals, not utterance time, once records carry effective time (RV04).
options.note: Depends on write-side event time with precision.

why: Anchoring to the read clock is wrong for any backfilled or historical store (G-W33, MIRIX and Combined show the same defect); RV04 separates utterance, ingestion and event time, so the leg should match event intervals with precision, falling back to B until that lands.

title: Entity leg and hub damping
question: How should an entity leg score hits so that frequently mentioned entities (the user, a partner) do not flood the pool?
today: entity_leg built and off (config/schema.py:1033); entity_expand_leg already damped; no hub penalty on entity_leg itself (G-W6 built-off).
others: Mem0: boost = sim x 0.5 x 1/(1 + 0.001(n-1)^2), capped, max over query entities. Hindsight: graph score tanh(0.5 x shared entities), at most 200 targets per entity. Cognee: up to 10 edges per entity hit.

options.label: Off (today)
options.detail: No entity leg; names reach the pool only via BM25.
options.note: Leaves the entity layer unused at read.

options.label: Entity leg with inverse-degree penalty
options.detail: Score falls with the entity's record count (Mem0 curve), capped boost, max over entities.
options.note: One curve constant to calibrate per store size.

options.label: Per-entity cap plus saturation
options.detail: Cap hits per entity and saturate the score (tanh) so convergent entities win.
options.note: Simple; hubs still take their full cap.

options.label: IDF-style weight learned from the store
options.detail: Weight each entity by log(N / records mentioning it), recomputed at sleep.
options.note: Self-calibrating; needs fresh counts.

why: G-W6 proposes the Mem0 penalty on the built leg, the smallest change with field evidence; screen it as router-activated (named subject in the contract) on the focus slice and a blind set.

title: Graph traversal method at read
question: Which graph traversal should the read use when the graph leg is active: BFS hops from seeds, one-hop link expansion with convergent scoring, personalised PageRank, or none?
today: Graph leg = BFS over entity hops, depth 2 (cap 3), max degree 50, at most 10 hits, trust-gated; PPR is a separate opt-in graph rerank; both off, the graph template turns the leg on (config/schema.py:699-719, engine.py:2609-2675). ADR-064/065 plan LadybugDB and Graphiti-style edges.
others: Hindsight: one hop from up to 20 semantic seeds, score = entity + semantic + causal link weights, 10 s timeout. Combined (Graphiti): BFS depth 3 inside edge search, RRF with BM25 and cosine. Cognee: k-hop neighbourhood from up to 10 seeds plus LLM-to-Cypher option.

options.label: Off by default (today)
options.detail: Graph exists for consolidation; reads ignore it.
options.note: Multi-hop relations go unfound.

options.label: BFS from seeds, depth 2
options.detail: Today's leg turned on: hops through entities, degree cap, trust gate.
options.note: Depth 2 brings noise on dense graphs.

options.label: One-hop convergent expansion
options.detail: Expand one hop from semantic seeds; score sums shared-entity, semantic and causal links so convergent evidence wins.
options.note: Bounded and cheap; misses two-hop chains.

options.label: Personalised PageRank over the seed subgraph
options.detail: PPR from query seeds ranks nodes by random-walk mass.
options.note: Good multi-hop; heavier compute, harder to explain.

why: The graph layer is unscreened (G-C3 arm written, not run) and must be fresh at read before deeper traversal pays (G-W49, G-W50); a bounded one-hop convergent leg is the cheapest testable step, with BFS depth 2 and PPR kept as advanced arms.

title: Episode and view-tag legs
question: How should derived units (episode narratives, session summaries, view tags) enter retrieval: as their own legs whose hits are lifted to sources, as competing text, or not at all?
today: Episode fragments built in window call 1 (off); when on they compete as raw text in the main pool, no dedicated episode leg (G-W1 built-off); view_tag_leg built and off (config/schema.py:1003); session_leg opt-in (config/schema.py:875).
others: EverMemOS: episode per cell is the retrieved unit, facts attached by parent id. Nemori: episodes and facts as two separate ranked lists. MemOS: summary and file memories with a 0.5 share kept. Memori: facts find, summaries come along attached.

options.label: Compete as raw text (today when on)
options.detail: Derived text mixed into the main pool.
options.note: Derived text can displace the evidence it summarises.

options.label: Episode leg lifted to parent turns
options.detail: Episodes are a retrieval key; hits map to their source turns (H-index), then optional notes arm.
options.note: Gains recall without adding unverified text.

options.label: Separate typed lists
options.detail: Return episodes and facts as their own sections.
options.note: No global budget; duplicate evidence.

options.label: Navigation only (summary first, drill down)
options.detail: Read summaries first, open sources on demand (progressive disclosure).
options.note: Fits agent hosts; needs a deep tier.

why: G-W1's own plan is the lifted episode leg first; it keeps raw sources authoritative (RV09) and feeds the single-score fusion of R-17; gate: beats facts-only on the focus slice or adds blind-slice value.

title: Fusion method across legs
question: How should leg results be fused: RRF, weighted score blend, per-shape weights, or a learned/calibrated combiner?
today: RRF k=60 whenever hybrid is on (config/constants.py:12); alternatives minmax, leg_weights and leg_weights_by_shape (config/schema.py:833-842); fusion cuts are the largest retrieval error class after recall (I75: 56 wrong answers, 23 with gold in a leg's top 10).
others: Hindsight, Honcho, Nemori, Mnemon: RRF k=60, equal weights. Mem0: additive semantic + sigmoid BM25 + entity, normalised by reachable maximum. Memori: linear blend 0.15 BM25 (0.30 for short queries). EverMemOS: RRF for order plus logistic calibration over dense and sparse scores.

options.label: RRF k=60 (today)
options.detail: Rank-only, scale-free, equal weights.
options.note: Robust; correlated legs double-vote.

options.label: Weighted score blend
options.detail: Normalised scores summed with fixed weights.
options.note: Weights tune easily to one dataset.

options.label: RRF with leg de-correlation
options.detail: RRF over independent source families; correlated legs merged before voting.
options.note: Fixes the double-vote without fitting weights.

options.label: Calibrated combiner
options.detail: Small logistic model over leg ranks/scores fitted per store on implicit feedback or probes.
options.note: Needs labels; overfitting risk on one benchmark.

why: I75 traced the loss to correlated voters and unprotected leg tops, not to the RRF formula; a learned combiner contradicts the generic, untuned rule of v2 unless trained on per-store signals.

title: Protected candidate pool policy
question: Should the fused pool reserve slots so each leg's or source family's best hits survive the cut, and how many?
today: pool_protect_per_leg defaults 0 (config/schema.py:447); per_leg N=3 screened +15 net on a full 1,540-question run (round 7 arm 1, every category up, about 30% more rerank cost); source_family mode built (config/schema.py:453), unscreened.
others: Hindsight: optional per-source cap after RRF. MemOS: keeps a 0.5 share for file memories. MIRIX: per-type top 10, no fusion. Mem0: drops keyword and entity hits outside the dense pool (the opposite).

options.label: No protection (today's default)
options.detail: Pool = fused top N.
options.note: BM25-only gold falls out.

options.label: Top N per leg protected
options.detail: Each leg's top 3 always enter the pool.
options.note: Measured +15 net; pool grows with leg count.

options.label: Per source family
options.detail: Reserve slots per independent family (dense, lexical, structured, derived), de-duplicated votes.
options.note: Pool size stays bounded as legs are added.

options.label: Quotas by memory type
options.detail: Fixed share per type in the final list.
options.note: Shares are static, not evidence-driven.

why: Per-leg protection is the strongest measured retrieval gain (+15 net, R02/I75a), but its pool grows with every new leg; source-family slots keep the gain bounded as R-05 and R-10 add legs. Screen C against B before adoption.

title: Leg floors and pool widening
question: How should per-leg score floors and candidate-pool size be set: fixed constants, scaled by store size, or widened adaptively when evidence is weak?
today: leg_min_scores per leg (config/schema.py:1024) logged as leg_floor cuts; candidate_pool multiplier 1..10 (config/schema.py:566); reranker pool fixed at about 20 whatever the haystack (I9 open: 'pool as a function of haystack size'); relevance_gate_regrow 2.0 widens only inside the gate.
others: Hindsight: arm depth set by budget level (100/300/1000). Mem0: dense top max(4 x top_k, 60) and a semantic floor 0.1 before fusion. Combined: fixed floors cosine 0.6/0.5, BM25 1.0. EverMemOS: cosine radius 0.5.

options.label: Fixed floors and pool (today)
options.detail: Constants per leg; pool about 20.
options.note: Floors do not transfer across embedding models (RV17).

options.label: Pool scaled by store size
options.detail: Pool = f(log N records), bounded min/max.
options.note: Large stores keep recall; reranker cost grows.

options.label: Pool by read tier
options.detail: Depth level sets pool size per leg.
options.note: Caller controls the cost knob.

options.label: Adaptive widening on weak evidence
options.detail: If the top score is below a store-calibrated band, double the pool once and re-fuse.
options.note: Second pass only when needed; tail latency.

why: Pool size is the main cost knob and I9 shows the fixed 20 ignores haystack size; tying it to the read tier (R-01) gives callers a predictable trade-off, while store-calibrated floors replace raw constants that do not transfer across models (RV17).

title: Default reranker model and placement
question: Which cross-encoder should be the v2 default reranker, if any, and should screening and production use the same one?
today: Engine rerank off by default (config/schema.py:333); best runs use Qwen3-Reranker-4B 4-bit (35 pairs/s); I84 offline: jina-reranker-v3.5 gold recall@10 0.822 vs 0.816 for the 4B, 196 pairs/s, adopted for screens only; reranker cut tokens per question 1,571 to 672.
others: Hindsight: local ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 on top 300 by default, Jina/Cohere/TEI optional. MemOS: bge-reranker-v2-m3 over HTTP. MemMachine: reranker required (qnli-electra-base default). EverMemOS: Qwen3-Reranker-4B in agentic only, calls it net-negative for multiround.

options.label: Off by default (today)
options.detail: Engine keeps the fused pool.
options.note: More reader tokens (about 2.3x).

options.label: Jina v3.5 default
options.detail: Light multilingual reranker on by default; 4B as a quality tier.
options.note: Matches the 4B on recall; licence terms to check for commercial use.

options.label: Qwen3-Reranker-4B default
options.detail: Today's best-run model on by default.
options.note: 5.6x slower than Jina; GPU memory.

options.label: Small CPU cross-encoder default
options.detail: MiniLM or bge-base on CPU; GPU models optional.
options.note: Gold recall@10 0.756-0.768, clearly below Jina.

why: I84 shows Jina v3.5 at parity with the 4B on gold recall (+0.006, CI spans 0) at 5.6x throughput, and the reranker roughly halves reader tokens; a light reference run on the focus slice is still required before Jina results are compared with 4B results.
owner_note: Standing owner decision (2026-10-11): jina-reranker-v3.5 is the reranker; no further reranker testing. Answer this only for when and where it runs, or confirm.

title: What the reranker scores
question: What unit should the reranker score: the single hit, the hit with neighbour context, or the whole expanded window that will be shown?
today: rerank_context 0..3 (config/schema.py:440) lets the reranker see neighbours, but replay windows are added after reranking (G-W28 partial); rerank_date_prefix opt-in; chunk-and-max for long turns opt-in (rerank_chunk_chars).
others: MemMachine: expands each hit (1/3 back, 2/3 forward) and reranks the window as one string. Hindsight: reranks single facts then multiplies recency and temporal proximity. Combined: built Cohere reranker never used.

options.label: Hit only, windows after (today)
options.detail: Rerank turns; expand afterwards.
options.note: Context-dependent turns ('yes, that one') score low.

options.label: Hit with neighbours as context
options.detail: Reranker sees neighbours, ranks the hit.
options.note: Longer documents per pair.

options.label: Whole dated window as the unit
options.detail: Rerank the window that will be shown; fill best-first under the budget; overlapping windows merged.
options.note: What is scored is what is shown; needs window de-duplication.

options.label: Chunk-and-max for long items
options.detail: Split long records and take the best chunk score.
options.note: Avoids silent tail truncation; complements C.

why: G-W28 proposes the MemMachine window unit and RV09 notes rerank_context already exists, so the remaining work is bounded integration; scoring the shown unit also makes R-18 packing consistent. Gate: focus slice multi-hop and temporal.

title: Recency, importance and reinforcement signals
question: Should non-relevance signals (recency, importance, reinforcement count) affect ranking, and if so additively, multiplicatively bounded, or only as tie-breakers?
today: Relevance-first: scoring recency_weight 0.0 and importance_weight 0.0 in the base template, record_access false (config/templates/base.yaml:20-26, ADR-030); semantic merge bumps importance +0.1 but the count is not used at read (G-W40 partial); trust_weighted_ranking true (config/schema.py:1494).
others: Hindsight: final = sigmoid(CE) x recency (-8%..+10%) x temporal proximity, never overriding relevance. Honcho: times_derived as an optional leg. Memori: num_times stored. Generative-agents style engines: additive w_rel, w_rec, w_imp.

options.label: Relevance only (today)
options.detail: Signals stored but weight 0.
options.note: Earlier additive weights demoted the best match.

options.label: Bounded multiplicative boosts
options.detail: Recency and reinforcement multiply the reranked score within a small band (for example 0.92-1.10).
options.note: Cannot override relevance; band must be generic.

options.label: Additive weighted score
options.detail: w_rel, w_rec, w_imp blend.
options.note: Measured harmful on stored transcripts.

options.label: Signals as separate legs
options.detail: Recency and most-reinforced as their own retrieval legs in fusion.
options.note: Adds voters; interacts with pool protection.

why: ADR-030 removed additive weights because they demoted the best match; G-W40 proposes Hindsight's bounded multiplicative boost, off by default until screened, so assistants with live preferences get freshness without benchmark tuning.

title: Evidence lifting and one score
question: How should hits from derived layers (facts, episodes, summaries, graph edges) be ranked against raw turns: lifted to parent sources under one score, calibrated scores per layer, or separate budgets?
today: Source-family pool built (R02); view_tags leg carries facts; facts_to_sources lifts derived hits to parent turns (config/schema.py:1014), off; derived layers not yet in the read path (G-W8 partial).
others: EverMemOS: heap-expand lets facts and episodes compete under one calibrated score. Memori: facts find, summaries fill. MemMachine: derivatives retrieved, mapped to episodes, then reranked as windows. Hindsight: prefer_observations drops raw facts already covered by an observation.

options.label: Separate per-layer lists
options.detail: No cross-layer score; each layer has its own k.
options.note: Duplicates evidence; no global choice.

options.label: Lift to parent turns, one reranked list
options.detail: Each derived hit maps to its source turns; sources rank under one reranker score; derived text kept only as capped notes.
options.note: Grounded; needs lineage on every derived row.

options.label: Calibrated mixed list
options.detail: Facts and raw units compete directly after per-layer score calibration.
options.note: Compact; calibration drifts per model.

options.label: Derived first, raw fill
options.detail: Show derived units, fill remaining budget with raw.
options.note: Extraction errors win the top slots.

why: G-W8 proposes lifting with family-protected fusion and derived text only as capped notes; it preserves raw authority (RV09) and makes the one reranker score meaningful across layers. Gate: focus slice with tokens within +30%.

title: Context budget and block shares
question: How should the context budget be enforced and split between blocks: one pool packed in rank order, fixed block shares, or dynamic shares that redistribute unused capacity?
today: Engine budget 2,048 tokens, top_k 16 (config/constants.py:210-212); header shares (lead, cards, profile, count) exist; real defect: assembly.py:288-299 stops packing at the first oversize item, and the first item can exceed the budget (RV08 confirmed); no per-block caps for derived layers.
others: Mnemon: 16 items / 12,000 chars with fixed per-block char caps (instructions 1,500, timelines 3,500). Hindsight: token-denominated rank-order packing, 4,096 fact tokens + 500 entities. Honcho: 40% summary / 60% recent messages. MemOS: floor + MMR + per-type quotas.

options.label: Today's packer with the break
options.detail: Single budget, stop at first oversize.
options.note: A long item evicts shorter useful ones.

options.label: Rank-order skip-and-continue, exact reader tokens
options.detail: Skip oversize items, truncate or fall back for the first, count headers and provenance, validate final prompt tokens with the reader tokenizer.
options.note: Pure fix; no share experiment needed.

options.label: B plus fixed block shares
options.detail: Raw >= 60%, notes <= 20%, summary/profile <= 10%, timelines <= 10%.
options.note: Shares unmeasured (RV08); idle share is wasted.

options.label: B plus dynamic shares with redistribution
options.detail: Caps per block, unused capacity flows to the next-best evidence in global rank order.
options.note: Needs paired screens at equal budget.

why: RV08 says fix packing first (B, adopt immediately as a correctness fix) and test shares separately; dynamic caps with redistribution keep derived blocks bounded (G-W25) without wasting budget when a block is empty.

title: Neighbour window expansion shape
question: How should a hit be expanded into context: fixed turn counts, asymmetric turn counts, token-sized windows, or windows scaled to the remaining budget?
today: Engine default 2 turns each side; arms 2 before / 4 after (config/schema.py:574-575); replay_window_unit turns|tokens (256/512 tokens), replay_budget_scaling and replay_hits_first opt-in (config/schema.py:582-594); over budget, neighbours of the worst hits drop first (D1 done).
others: MemMachine: 1/3 backward, 2/3 forward, default 0 in API, 3 in its eval script. MemOS: neighbor_discovery off, adjacent chunks at 0.8 x relevance. Nemori: verbatim source turns of the top-2 episodes only.

options.label: Fixed symmetric turns (engine default)
options.detail: k turns either side.
options.note: Long turns blow the budget, short ones under-fill.

options.label: Asymmetric forward-biased turns
options.detail: More turns after the hit than before (answers follow questions).
options.note: Conversation-specific; documents differ.

options.label: Token-sized, budget-scaled windows
options.detail: Window measured in tokens, shrunk as the budget fills, merged when overlapping.
options.note: Generic across chats and documents.

options.label: Segment-bounded windows
options.detail: Expand to the topic segment or episode boundary the hit belongs to, capped.
options.note: Coherent units; needs the window segmenter on.

why: Token-sized windows work for any workload (long document chunks, short chat turns) and pair with exact-token packing (R-18) and window reranking (R-15); the forward bias can remain a per-template preset rather than an engine default.

title: Rendering format, order and dates
question: How should the composed context be rendered for the reader: plain text in relevance order, dated lines in chronological order, or structured sections with provenance and a query-contract header?
today: Engine render plain by default (config/schema.py:625); dated lines come from the harness adapter; chat@dated prompt in base template; present_order relevance|recorded (config/schema.py:1087); replay chronological; stable prefix before volatile records (core/policies/assembly.py:80-85).
others: MemMachine: '[Weekday, Month DD, YYYY at HH:MM] producer: content' in chronological order. MIRIX: typed XML sections with 'k out of N items'. Memori: '- fact. Stated at date' plus summaries. Mnemon: coarse-to-fine View blocks.

options.label: Plain, engine leaves dates to caller (today)
options.detail: Engine renders text; adapters add dates.
options.note: Every integrator re-solves date rendering.

options.label: Dated chronological lines in the engine
options.detail: Engine renders absolute dates with weekday and speaker, chronological per window.
options.note: Small token overhead (+7% date prefixes measured, D1).

options.label: Typed sections with provenance tags
options.detail: Raw evidence, notes, profile, public knowledge as labelled sections; each line carries source id, speaker, date precision and modality.
options.note: Lets the reader tell inference from observation (A08).

options.label: C plus contract header and integer aliases
options.detail: One-line query contract header; records shown with short aliases mapped back in code.
options.note: Header is the part of A03 that measured +9.

why: The engine should own date and provenance rendering so modality, speaker and coarse precision survive to the reader (RV03, RV04, A08); the A03 header measured net +9 at zero cost, and aliases keep prompts short (G-W36).

title: Relevance gate and abstention
question: How should the read decide that memory has nothing relevant and return an empty or flagged context?
today: relevance_gate off|decider|store_calibrated (config/schema.py:1231): store_calibrated scores 20 off-topic probes and passes only if raw top > p95 + 1.0 sd, named-entity bypass; built, never screened; decider form screened r3d (OP-Bench +22, a recall set -4 net inside band); always-on theta_abstain 0.25 on composite scores is defeated by min-max reranking unless abstain_on_raw (config/constants.py:125).
others: Memori: relevance threshold 0.1; nothing injected if none passes. MemOS: drops relativity < 0.45. Hindsight: similarity floors only, always returns the top fact. Cognee: skips the answer call when every lane is empty.

options.label: Theta on composite only (today)
options.detail: Fixed abstain threshold, mostly inert after min-max rerank.
options.note: Irrelevant memory is injected into unrelated requests.

options.label: Fixed score threshold
options.detail: Absolute floor on the top score.
options.note: Threshold does not transfer across models or stores.

options.label: Store-calibrated gate with named bypass
options.detail: Probe distribution per store sets the bar; named references bypass; returns empty context with a reason.
options.note: Zero calls; global gate may suppress multi-hop evidence.

options.label: Small decider model
options.detail: A local classifier (about 25 ms CPU) judges whether memory can supply the slot.
options.note: Measured on one set; extra model dependency.

why: P01 shows memory injected regardless of the request hurts personalisation sets (OP-Bench irrelevant 14.1); the store-calibrated gate is generic and zero-call, but must be screened for no recall loss on all-on-topic sets (MAB, ConvoMem) and report its fired rate per slice.

title: Agentic multi-step read design
question: What form should the deep tier's multi-step read take: rewrite loop, missing-slot loop with typed actions, tool-calling agent, or read-time fact chaining?
today: All off: agentic_mode query (I67) or slot (E02: one action per missing slot: memory_search, relation_expand, neighbor_lookup, calculate), max 2 steps, multi_hop trigger, 0.6 of budget kept for step 0 (config/schema.py:1154-1222). f-slot-i2: net -3 (+1/-4), fired 150/437, about 8x wall time, not adopted; fact chain f-chain-i2 net -1.
others: Hindsight reflect: tool agent (search_mental_models, recall, expand, done), up to 10 iterations, 300 s cap. Honcho dialectic: 1-10 iterations by level. MemMachine: ChainOfQuery up to 3 rewrites after sufficiency check. Mnemon: judge-act loop paging unmet needs.

options.label: Slot loop, opt-in (today)
options.detail: Typed missing-slot actions with caps.
options.note: No gain where it fired.

options.label: Sufficiency check plus one rewrite round
options.detail: One judge call; if insufficient, one rewritten search, then answer.
options.note: Cheapest deep step; modest ceiling.

options.label: Tool-calling agent over memory APIs
options.detail: The deep tier exposes search, expand, timeline and calculate tools to the caller's model with caps.
options.note: Flexible for agents; hardest to evaluate.

options.label: No engine loop; expose tools only
options.detail: Engine stays single-shot; host agent drives repeated reads (progressive disclosure).
options.note: Pushes cost and policy to the host.

why: Two screened loops (E02 net -3, E01 net -1) gave no gain and RV12 calls the evidence inconclusive at high cost; v2 should keep engine reads single-shot and offer bounded tool endpoints for agent hosts, retaining the slot loop as an opt-in research arm.

title: External public knowledge at read
question: Should a read join private memory with external public knowledge, and under what policy?
today: read.external_evidence off|cache|web (config/schema.py:1300) with external_provider none|http|wikipedia, call budget 20, privacy filter, separate '[public knowledge]' block with a never-proves-private-facts clause; invited-inference trigger gates it (A08); built, opt-in, unscreened (E03).
others: MemOS: internet leg exists, off by default (fine-mode intent). Hindsight, Honcho, Mem0: none in the memory read. Cognee: none at read; external data enters only through ingestion.

options.label: Never at read
options.detail: Memory engine returns only stored evidence; the host agent does web search.
options.note: Cleanest privacy story.

options.label: Opt-in, gated, separate block (today)
options.detail: Only for invited-inference questions, privacy-filtered query, cached, cited separately.
options.note: Useful for recommendations; query may leak context.

options.label: Cache-only public knowledge
options.detail: Only pre-fetched or locally indexed public sources; no live calls at read.
options.note: Deterministic and private; coverage limited.

options.label: Ingest public knowledge as resource memory
options.detail: Public documents become a resource-type store read like any other leg, labelled by provenance class.
options.note: Unifies the read path; needs provenance labels.

why: The owner approved E03 behind an opt-in flag; RV13 requires external sources only for general world knowledge, never private history, and benchmark modes must keep external-tool results separate, which B already enforces.

title: As-of reads and default time view
question: What time view should a read use by default (current valid state, all history, or a caller-given as-of), and how should superseded records appear?
today: Reads accept as_of and valid-time / record-time range filters (core/read_filters.py:245-260, engine.py:6595-6602); _current_at checks begun-by, ended-after, not retracted, not quarantined (engine.py:1097); default is current state; superseded history is not shown alongside current values.
others: Graphiti (Combined): valid_at / invalid_at on edges, search returns current edges. Mnemon: value histories shown with a 'no longer current' withdrawal. Hindsight: occurred vs mentioned dates. Mem0, Memori: overwrite or delete, no history at read.

options.label: Current state, as-of on request (today)
options.detail: Superseded records hidden unless as_of points before supersession.
options.note: Questions about change ('used to', 'before') miss history.

options.label: Current plus compact value history
options.detail: Show the current value with prior values and dates as a short history line ('changed from A to B on ...').
options.note: Small token cost; reader sees transitions.

options.label: Contract-driven time view
options.detail: Time scope in the query contract selects current, history or as-of automatically.
options.note: Relies on contract accuracy for time scope.

options.label: All history, reader decides
options.detail: Return all versions, newest first.
options.note: Stale values confuse the reader.

why: MemSpine is the only surveyed engine with full bitemporal fields (layers table), so the read should use them: the A03 contract already carries time scope, and B's history line is the fallback rendering when scope is unclear (RV04, RV05 A to B to A states).

title: Read latency targets and parallel legs
question: What latency budget should the default read commit to, and should legs run in parallel to meet it?
today: Legs and probes run sequentially (no gather), reranker batches of 8 in a worker thread (engine.py:4270; memspine.json speed row); no stated read p50/p95 target; graph BFS target d3 p95 < 100 ms only (ADR-015); reports require p50/p95 per run (GAP_TO_SOLUTION_PLAN.md:217).
others: Hindsight: arms run in parallel, 10 s graph timeout drops the arm. Nemori: episodes and facts searched with asyncio.gather, search 787 ms. MemOS: legs in parallel. Mnemon: p50 9.6 s with planner and judge calls.

options.label: No target, sequential legs (today)
options.detail: Latency is whatever the enabled legs cost.
options.note: Each new leg adds its full time.

options.label: Parallel legs, per-leg timeout
options.detail: Legs gathered concurrently; a leg past its timeout is dropped and logged.
options.note: Needs thread-safe stores and a deterministic order.

options.label: B plus tier SLOs
options.detail: Publish p95 targets per tier (for example fast < 150 ms without reranker, standard < 500 ms with a light reranker on GPU) and test them in CI.
options.note: Makes regressions visible; hardware-dependent numbers.

options.label: Anytime read
options.detail: Return the best context found by a deadline; late legs refine a cached result.
options.note: Non-deterministic results.

why: As router-activated legs (R-05) and the graph leg arrive, sequential execution adds every leg's time; RV10 asks for reproducible p50/p95 at matched load, so tier targets give the screens a cost limit to check against.

title: Read-path caching and invalidation
question: What should the read path cache (query vectors, leg results, reranker scores, composed contexts, prompt prefixes), and how is the cache invalidated on writes and forget?
today: Per-read snapshot, vocabulary and vector caches; query vectors cached (engine.py:739-776, 1268-1300); cache backends memory|disk|redis|valkey with namespace prefix (config/schema.py:1369); no composed-context or rerank-score cache; stable prefix first for provider caching (G-W45 partial); RV07 flags lineage not surviving restart in persistent caches.
others: Mnemon: republishes an unchanged View to keep the provider cache warm; per-snapshot BM25 cache. Hindsight: bank-agnostic cached system prefix with provider breakpoints. Honcho: no read result cache noted.

options.label: Embeddings and snapshots only (today)
options.detail: Cache inputs, recompute ranking each read.
options.note: Safe; repeated questions pay full rerank.

options.label: Rerank-score cache keyed by (query, record version, model)
options.detail: Pairs reused across repeated or similar reads; invalidated by record version.
options.note: Reranker is the main read cost.

options.label: Composed-context cache with generation stamps
options.detail: Whole context cached per (namespace generation, query, tier); any write or forget bumps the generation.
options.note: Stale or post-erasure leaks if a bump is missed.

options.label: A plus provider prompt-cache layout
options.detail: Keep variable content last in every prompt; cache hints when a hosted reader is bound.
options.note: Gain small on local models (prefill ~10%).

why: Caching composed results raises the erasure risk RV07 and RV21 warn about (tombstones and generation checks needed); prompt-layout caching (G-W45) is free and safe, and B can follow once cache scope includes tenant, record version and model.

title: One model or a model per role
question: Should v2 bind one generative model for every internal role, or route each role (extract, window, judge, summarise, reader) to a model sized for it?
today: Per-role binding through LiteLLM: llm.roles maps 22 prompt roles (prompts/roles.py PROMPT_ROLES) to an LLMRoleConfig each (config/schema.py:193-215); roles absent are disabled. In practice evals bind one Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M via Ollama for writer, reader and judge (evals/QWEN_STACK_RESULTS.md).
others: Mnemon: a cheap System-1 model reads ~35k tokens per question, the answer model sees a 12k-char View. Hindsight: one LLM for retain/consolidate/reflect with per-operation temperatures. Mem0: one LLM plus an optional LLM reranker. LightMem: small local models (LLMLingua-2, topic encoder) before one hosted extractor.

options.label: One model for all roles
options.detail: A single binding serves every role; per-role entries only override temperature and max tokens.
options.note: Simplest to run and reason about; the cheap high-volume roles pay large-model prices.

options.label: Per-role binding, one default (today)
options.detail: Every role may name its own model; unnamed roles fall back to one default binding.
options.note: Flexible, but nothing tells a deployer which roles deserve a small model.

options.label: Two tiers: small worker, large reader
options.detail: Ship two named tiers: 'worker' (window extract, summarise, resolve, dedupe; 1-4B or a 9B quantised) and 'reader' (answer, judge, reflect); roles map to a tier by default and can still be pinned.
options.note: Most write volume runs on the cheap tier; needs a quality screen per role before a small model is the default.

options.label: Cascade with escalation
options.detail: The small tier answers first; low confidence, validation failure or a conflict escalates the item to the large tier.
options.note: Pays large-model cost only on hard items; confidence from small models is poorly calibrated.

why: Write-side roles dominate call volume (one call per window, sleep batches of 30-50) while answer quality is set by the reader; a named two-tier map keeps B's flexibility but makes the cheap default explicit. RV15 applies: any role moved to the small tier needs an extraction screen, not just CPU tests.

title: Local-first or hosted model default
question: Which provider class is the shipped default and supported path for write-side roles: in-process/local open weights, a local server, or a hosted API?
today: Local by decision (BD-5): Ollama Qwen via LiteLLM, or llamacpp/<gguf> in process (services/llm/llama_cpp.py, [llmlocal]); hosted providers work through LiteLLM; consent.remote_llm_max_tier withholds high-tier record text from remote providers (services/llm/tier_gate.py).
others: Memori: every exchange goes to a closed hosted extractor. Hindsight and Mem0: hosted by default (OpenAI-compatible), local optional. LightMem: local compression and segmentation on GPU, hosted extractor. Mnemon: host agent's model.

options.label: Local server default (today)
options.detail: Ollama/vLLM on loopback is the documented default; hosted is opt-in and tier-gated.
options.note: Private and free per call; quality capped by local model size and GPU.

options.label: In-process default
options.detail: llama.cpp in process as the default; no server to run; enables KV reuse (BD-7).
options.note: No IPC and prefix reuse, but model memory lives in the engine process.

options.label: Hosted default, local optional
options.detail: OpenAI-compatible hosted model by default; local as an extra.
options.note: Best out-of-box quality; every user turn leaves the host.

options.label: Split by sensitivity
options.detail: Write-side roles that read raw turns stay local; reader may be hosted, fed only tier-gated context.
options.note: Raw transcripts never leave; answers can use a stronger model.

why: BD-5 keeps extraction local for privacy, and the tier gate already wraps remote roles; making the split explicit lets a deployment buy answer quality without sending raw turns out. A stays the zero-config profile.

title: Behaviour when no model is configured
question: When a feature needs an LLM role that is not bound, should the engine fail at start, degrade to a model-free path, or run with a weaker local substitute?
today: Slim core (D-03): read and write make zero LLM calls by default; a feature whose role is missing fails hard at start() (window_extract: engine.py:13705-13713); extraction can fall back to rules or GLiNER2 (D-28, [ner]).
others: Mnemon: raw record path has zero LLM calls; consolidation optional. memU: engine makes no LLM calls; host agent does distillation. Mem0 and Cognee: require an LLM for add().

options.label: Fail fast at start (today)
options.detail: Missing role for an enabled feature raises ConfigError; no silent degradation.
options.note: Honest; a small config mistake blocks start.

options.label: Degrade with a named mode
options.detail: Start succeeds; the feature runs its model-free path (rules, GLiNER2, extractive summary) and describe() reports 'degraded: window_extract -> rules'.
options.note: Always runs; users may not notice lower-quality derived layers.

options.label: Bundle a tiny local default
options.detail: Ship an auto-downloaded 0.5-1.5B GGUF used when nothing is bound.
options.note: Zero-config LLM, but a large download and weak output by surprise.

options.label: Fail fast, with explicit fallback key
options.detail: A per-feature 'on_missing_model: error|rules|skip' key, default error.
options.note: Keeps today's safety and lets an operator choose degradation deliberately.

why: D-03 keeps the core model-free; fail-fast prevents silently empty derived layers, and an explicit key covers edge devices and CI without a surprise download.

title: Structured output method
question: How should structured write-side outputs be obtained: prompt-described JSON parsed and repaired in code, provider JSON mode, schema-constrained decoding, or tool calls?
today: Prompt-described JSON/YAML with a pydantic output_model per prompt, json-repair safety net (services/llm/base.py:43), per-section validation; constrained decoding exists only as an opt-in on the retry (llm.structured.constrained_retry, config/schema.py:218-229, default off).
others: Hindsight: pydantic json_schema response_format (optionally strict). Mem0, Nemori, LightMem: json_object mode plus fence stripping. MIRIX: every write is a tool call with a pydantic schema. Mnemon: line protocols (SEARCH:, NOTE:) with a tolerant parser.

options.label: Prompted JSON + code repair (today)
options.detail: Model writes JSON from instructions; json-repair and per-section validation in code.
options.note: Works on any backend; parse failures cost a section.

options.label: JSON mode
options.detail: response_format json_object when the backend supports it; schema stays in the prompt.
options.note: Guarantees valid JSON, not the right keys.

options.label: Schema-constrained decoding by default
options.detail: json_schema / GBNF grammar from the pydantic model on every call; prompt-only fallback for backends that refuse.
options.note: Removes parse failures; strict grammars can push small models into empty or truncated lists.

options.label: Tool calls
options.detail: Each output kind is a function the model calls.
options.note: Natural for agents, verbose and multi-turn for batch extraction.

why: Ollama, vLLM and llama.cpp all accept a JSON schema, so constrained decoding is available on the local stack; it removes the sections_dropped class that today's fail-closed path counts. Gate per RV11: per-item validation still runs and truncation must be detected, not hidden.

title: Repair after an invalid reply
question: When part of a structured reply fails validation, should v2 drop it, re-ask for only the failed part with the validator's errors, or re-run the whole call?
today: Fail closed per section; a schema-invalid section is dropped and counted; auto-split after repeated joint failures (workers/windows.py:618-639); optional single plain retry (llm.structured.retry_on_error, default off).
others: Hindsight: re-ask listing keys used versus valid keys, auto-split on output overflow. Honcho deriver: 3 retries in json_mode. MIRIX: tool-error guidance ('id cannot be found, recheck ids'). Mem0/Nemori: no repair.

options.label: Drop and count (today)
options.detail: Invalid sections or items are discarded and counted in window_stats.
options.note: Cheap and safe; loses valid content that was one bad key away.

options.label: Diagnostic re-ask for failed part
options.detail: One retry carrying the validator errors, for failed sections/items only; new items forbidden and diffed against the failed output.
options.note: Recovers most near-misses; a second call on a minority of windows.

options.label: Whole-call retry
options.detail: Re-run the same prompt up to N times.
options.note: Simple; repeats valid work and may fail the same way.

options.label: Per-item validation, then targeted re-ask
options.detail: Validate items independently, keep valid ones at once, re-ask only for invalid ones, persist failure reason and retry eligibility.
options.note: Best yield per token; needs item-level ids and a persisted retry state.

why: RV11: a unified item list must not lose a batch to one bad item; G-P4's re-ask is the repair step. Gate: sections_dropped down, no new ungrounded items.

title: Output serialisation format
question: Which output serialisation should write prompts use by default: JSON, YAML, a compact positional line protocol, or the format the decoder can constrain?
today: Per prompt: format json or yaml (prompts/base.py:8, 'yaml/cod are token-lean vs json'); window_extract is json (window_extract.yaml:4); extract@session* are YAML.
others: Mnemon: line protocols (KIND:, NEED:, [e#]). Mem0/Hindsight/Nemori/LightMem: JSON. memU: free text or YAML front matter.

options.label: Mixed per prompt (today)
options.detail: Each prompt picks json or yaml.
options.note: Two parsers and two repair paths.

options.label: JSON everywhere
options.detail: One format, compatible with schema-constrained decoding.
options.note: Quotes and braces cost 10-25% more output tokens than YAML.

options.label: Compact keys JSON
options.detail: JSON with one- or two-letter keys (s, r, o, kind, lines) mapped to full names in code.
options.note: Constrainable and lean; short keys are less self-describing to small models.

options.label: Line protocol
options.detail: One item per line with fixed fields separated by a delimiter.
options.note: Cheapest decode; nested fields and escaping get fragile.

why: Decode dominates call time locally (Qwen3.5-9B decode 115 tok/s vs prefill 4,869 tok/s, QWEN_STACK_RESULTS), so output tokens are the cost lever, and JSON keeps P-04's constrained decoding. G-W49's prompt v2 already uses compact keys.

title: Examples in prompts
question: Should shipped prompts contain worked examples, and if so of what kind?
today: One invented single-line example per prompt with made-up names (extract@session4.yaml:45-49); window_extract has inline fragments (a specific brand-name example); CI gold-lint denies known benchmark strings in defaults/*.yaml only.
others: Mnemon: no few-shot at all. Mem0: ~11 worked examples, some LoCoMo-shaped. Nemori and LightMem: examples that reproduce benchmark facts (leak). Hindsight: generic examples with 'never emit their facts' guard.

options.label: One invented example (today)
options.detail: A single made-up example per prompt, linted.
options.note: Shape guidance; small models may copy example content.

options.label: No examples, shape only
options.detail: Rules plus the output schema; no example content anywhere.
options.note: Zero leak and copy risk; relies on the schema and constrained decoding for shape.

options.label: Rich few-shot
options.detail: Several input/output pairs per prompt.
options.note: Helps weak models; leak and anchoring risk, longer prefix.

options.label: Examples as negative contrasts only
options.detail: Short 'X, not Y' contrasts inside rules, no full input/output pairs.
options.note: Teaches the rule without a copyable item.

why: The examples that leaked benchmark material across five engines (prompt matrix F18) are the main contamination path; G-W49 v2 (353 tokens, no examples) shows a shape-only prompt is viable once P-04 constrains the shape. Contrasts (D) stay allowed if gold-linted.

title: Cache-friendly prompt layout
question: What layout rule should every prompt follow so provider and local prefix caches can reuse the static part?
today: Static system block first, variable transcript/question last; but window_extract's system text varies with the configured sections ({{ sections | join }}), and no cache hints are sent (G-W45 partial; prompt matrix F22).
others: Hindsight: bank mission moved into the user turn so one cached prefix serves all banks; provider breakpoints. Mnemon: note listing kept in first-seen order as a cacheable prefix, measures stable prefix length. MemOS and MIRIX: date and memories inside the system prompt, short prefix.

options.label: Static-first convention (today)
options.detail: Variables last by habit; no check.
options.note: Drifts as prompts change; section switches already break it.

options.label: Enforced byte-stable prefix
options.detail: The system part may not reference any variable; a unit test renders every prompt under two contexts and asserts identical prefixes; mode switches move into the user part.
options.note: Cheap guarantee; small local prefill gain (~10% of call time).

options.label: B plus provider cache hints
options.detail: Add cache_control/breakpoints when a hosted provider is bound, and keep llama.cpp/vLLM prefix caching on.
options.note: Large saving on hosted calls; provider-specific code.

options.label: Stable prefix including stable data
options.detail: Also keep slowly changing data (profile card, known names) in first-seen order before the transcript.
options.note: Longer reuse; reordering data to fit the cache can change model behaviour.

why: Locally prefill is ~10% of call time (G-W45), so B's test is the main value; hosted readers (P-02 D) make cache hints worthwhile. RV10 asks that prefix-cache state be logged with every latency claim.

title: Identifiers shown to the model
question: How should records, lines and entities shown to a model be referenced: raw ids, per-call integer aliases, or names only?
today: Turns appear as [n]; an out-of-range citation is dropped silently and counted as facts_uncited, so an invented alias looks like a missing one; no shipped prompt shows a raw record id yet (G-W36).
others: Mem0: swaps UUIDs for 0-9. Hindsight: short aliases and scrubs ids the model never saw. Graphiti (Combined): continuous integer index across two candidate lists. MIRIX: raw ids with 'recheck ids' repair.

options.label: Line numbers only (today)
options.detail: [n] for lines; records never shown.
options.note: Fine until neighbours or known facts appear in the prompt (G-W4).

options.label: Per-call integer aliases, strict
options.detail: Every shown record/line gets a small integer or prefixed alias ([k3], [3]); a reply citing an unshown alias is rejected and counted separately.
options.note: Short tokens, zero invented ids.

options.label: Raw ids
options.detail: Show stored ids directly.
options.note: Long tokens; models mangle UUIDs and leak internal ids.

options.label: Names only, resolved in code
options.detail: Show entity names; code resolves names to ids.
options.note: Natural for entities; ambiguous for homonyms (RV17).

why: G-W36 gate is zero invented ids; aliases are needed once G-W4/G-W49 show known items. Names (D) stay for entities alongside aliased records.

title: Language of stored items
question: In which language should write prompts produce memory items when the conversation is not in English?
today: No write prompt has a language rule (G-P1 missing); a non_english preset exists (config/presets/non_english.yaml) but prompts do not instruct; keys and enum values are English.
others: Hindsight: same language and script, never translate. Mem0: input-language block. EverMemOS: language module at head and tail of each prompt. MemOS: language detection per item.

options.label: No rule (today)
options.detail: Model chooses; small models often translate to English.
options.note: Silent translation loses names and quoted words.

options.label: Same language, shared partial
options.detail: One partial in every write prompt: write each item in the language of its lines, never translate names, titles or quoted words; keys and enums stay English.
options.note: Cross-lingual retrieval then depends on a multilingual embedder (P-17).

options.label: Canonical language plus original
options.detail: Store item in a deployment language and keep the original span.
options.note: Uniform retrieval; doubles output and translation errors enter memory.

options.label: Detect and route
options.detail: Detect language per window and pick a language-specific prompt variant.
options.note: Best per language; many prompts to maintain and lint.

why: Generic rule with no extra calls; must be paired with RV15's screen (English output unchanged on the focus slice) and a multilingual embedder choice.

title: Length rules for items and outputs
question: How should item length and total output length be bounded: hard caps, soft guidance with warnings, or per-type budgets?
today: token_budget per prompt sent as max_tokens (160-4096; window_extract 4096); episode fields bounded; a fact's value is not (G-P3, prompt matrix F10); temperature 0 for the window writer (workers/windows.py:116-118).
others: Mem0: 15-80 words per fact. Hindsight: 1-2 sentences, auto-split on output overflow. Mnemon: events at most 30 words; maxTokens 200-1000 per call. EverMemOS: ~50-word summary with a 3-tier repair.

options.label: Output cap only (today)
options.detail: max_tokens per prompt; no per-item rule.
options.note: Run-on facts; a hit cap truncates silently.

options.label: Hard per-item word cap
options.detail: Validator drops or cuts items over N words.
options.note: RV15: erases lists and conditions.

options.label: Soft per-item guidance + warn
options.detail: 'one sentence, about 40 words; split longer statements', self-contained rule first; validator warns and counts, does not drop; list members kept.
options.note: Shorter items without losing content; needs a counter.

options.label: C plus truncation detection
options.detail: Also detect finish_reason=length and schedule the remaining lines as a new window instead of discarding.
options.note: No silent coverage loss (RV11).

why: RV15 rejects hard caps; RV11 requires a cap to expose or reschedule coverage loss. G-P3 gate: grounding unchanged, mean fact length down.

title: Prompt and model identity in provenance
question: What identity should each derived record and cached reply carry so prompt or model changes are traceable and invalidate caches correctly?
today: Prompt version (auto-bumped on override, plus a partials fingerprint suffix, prompts/registry.py:102-126) enters E3 cache keys and SourceInfo.prompt_version; the window call cache keys on (model, prompt version, sections, transcript, participants) (workers/windows.py:648-667); no rendered-prompt hash or decoding settings recorded.
others: Graphiti (Combined): pins nothing per record. Hindsight: per-operation config in logs. Honcho: per-call token telemetry. None found records a rendered prompt hash per derived item.

options.label: Prompt id@version (today)
options.detail: Version and partials fingerprint; model name only in the window cache key.
options.note: Misses model, quantisation, decoding and input-block changes (RV07).

options.label: Derivation fingerprint
options.detail: Hash of rendered static prompt + schema version + model id + quantisation + decoding settings + input block set; stored on each derived record and in every cache key.
options.note: Exact invalidation and re-derivation targeting; slightly larger records.

options.label: B plus run manifest
options.detail: Also emit a per-run manifest (tokenizer, template, cache state, tokens, retries, queue delay) for any reported number.
options.note: Reproducible claims (RV10); more bookkeeping.

why: RV07 (cache identity must include prompt/schema/model and all input blocks) and RV10 (claims need a reproducible manifest) both require it; it is also the hook P-25 uses to find records to re-derive.

title: Gold-lint scope and strictness
question: What should the prompt contamination lint screen, and should it block CI or warn?
today: tests/unit/test_prompt_gold_lint.py denies known multi-word benchmark answers and speaker names in defaults/*.yaml only; _partials/*.j2, single-word tokens and user overrides are not screened (G-P5 partial).
others: Mnemon: no examples, nothing to lint. Nemori, LightMem, EverMemOS, MemOS: benchmark names or facts in shipped prompts (prompt matrix F18). No engine found ships a lint.

options.label: Known strings in YAML (today)
options.detail: Deny-list of multi-word answers and speaker names.
options.note: Misses partials and single-word leaks.

options.label: Every capitalised token and quoted word
options.detail: Screen all prompt files and partials against benchmark answer and speaker vocabularies with an allow-list of invented names (Ilse, Bram); blocking.
options.note: Some false positives to allow-list.

options.label: B plus rendered prompts and overrides
options.detail: Also lint rendered prompts in eval runs and config overrides at start (warn).
options.note: Catches leaks via config, not just shipped files.

why: The I80 contamination incident and RV12 (pre-I80 results contaminated) show leaks cost whole result sets; overrides are the untested path.

title: Write-side call and token targets
question: What call-count and token targets should v2 commit to for writing, per turn and per derived layer?
today: Zero LLM calls by default; window mode one call for up to three layers on at most 6 turns / 1,500 tokens (LoCoMo mean 186 input tokens); facts_graph prompt 958 tokens; sleep batches 30 summaries / 50 resolutions per call (memspine.json token_economy).
others: LightMem: ~255-415 write calls for LoCoMo vs 5.5-19k for Mem0/A-Mem. Mem0: one call per add() with an ~8.5k-token static prompt. Graphiti: 2 calls per episode plus one per new fact (RV18). Honcho: tiny static prompt per 1,024-token batch.

options.label: No targets, measure only (today)
options.detail: Counters exist; no stated budget.
options.note: Costs creep as features land.

options.label: Stated targets per layer
options.detail: Targets: <= 1 call per window (all online layers), static prompt <= 500 tokens, output <= 2x input; sleep work amortised to <= 0.2 calls per turn; checked in the eval manifest.
options.note: Keeps the economy visible; targets can push quality-losing cuts.

options.label: Hard write token budget
options.detail: Per-namespace token budget per hour/day; extraction stops or defers when spent.
options.note: Bounded spend; deferred derivation must be durable (G-W27).

options.label: B with an optional C
options.detail: Targets as regression gates; hard budget off by default.
options.note: Default economy plus a cap for paid deployments.

why: G-W49 v2 (353-token prompt, one item list per batch) sets a measurable target; RV11 notes one call is a target, not an observed total, so the gate measures retries and split calls too.

title: Thinking mode per role
question: Should reasoning ('thinking') be off, on, or chosen per role and per call?
today: no_think defaults on for qwen3 ids (services/llm/litellm_llm.py:34; config/schema.py:211-215); <think> blocks stripped from every reply; Qwen3.5 needs reasoning_effort none. Measured on 152 questions: thinking on matched off on the 103 both answered (0.806 vs 0.806) at 5.7x run time and 22x tokens, 49 truncated.
others: Honcho dialectic: five reasoning levels chosen per call. Hindsight: reflect at temperature 0.9, retain at 0.1, no thinking. Mnemon: temperature 0 everywhere.

options.label: Off everywhere (today)
options.detail: Thinking disabled for every role; tags stripped.
options.note: Measured no loss on answers; may lose on multi-step consolidation.

options.label: Per role default
options.detail: Off for write and answer; allowed with a token cap for judge, reflect and consolidation where a wrong merge is costly.
options.note: Spends reasoning only where errors persist in memory.

options.label: Per-call depth level
options.detail: Caller passes a depth level; thinking budget scales with it.
options.note: Flexible; overlaps the read-tier choice (G-W41).

options.label: On everywhere
options.detail: Let reasoning models think on every call.
options.note: Truncations and parse failures in structured roles.

why: The paired test shows no answer gain at 5.7x time, so answer and write stay off; background roles are off the hot path and judge a merge once for many reads. Needs a screen before enabling.

title: Compression before model calls
question: Should transcripts be compressed locally before the write call, and should retrieved context be compressed before the reader?
today: Write: transcript sent as written (G-W31 missing). Read: optional assembly-time LLMLingua stage after drop_lowest_score ([compress] extra; core/policies/compression.py:56), off by default.
others: LightMem: LLMLingua-2 drops 20-40% of each message before extraction; same encoder segments topics. MIRIX: compresses the conversation to a keyword topic string before retrieval. MemOS: optional query-conditioned LLM 'recreate' pass.

options.label: None on write, opt-in on read (today)
options.detail: Raw transcript into extraction; LLMLingua only at assembly when enabled.
options.note: Windows are already small (mean 186 tokens).

options.label: Opt-in write compressor port
options.detail: Pluggable compressor before call 1 (LLMLingua-2 on CPU/GPU), off by default, enabled only for long-turn workloads (documents, tool output).
options.note: Saves on long inputs; can drop the detail a fact needs.

options.label: Extractive trim only
options.detail: Rule-based removal of filler, boilerplate and repeated quoted text; no model.
options.note: Safe but small gains; hard cuts lose tails.

options.label: Read-side only, budget-driven
options.detail: Never compress before extraction; compress retrieved context only when it exceeds the reader budget after packing.
options.note: Grounded spans stay verbatim in memory.

why: Span-grounded extraction needs verbatim lines, so compression stays off by default; G-W31's gate (grounding rate unchanged, tokens down) decides per workload, and long document or tool-output turns are where it can pay.

title: Default embedding model and host
question: Which embedding model and runtime should be the default: small CPU ONNX, a larger GPU model, or a hosted embedder?
today: fastembed BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (384-d, CPU ONNX) default (config/schema.py:96-105); st and litellm providers available. Measured: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B +2.1 points retrieval sufficiency (0.615 vs 0.594) at the same wall-clock; GPU batch 32 is 80-90x cheaper per token than batch 1.
others: EverMemOS: MRL-truncated 1,024-d. Mem0, Hindsight: OpenAI-compatible hosted default. LightMem: local GPU embedder. Mnemon: lazy embedding at first search.

options.label: Small CPU English model (today)
options.detail: bge-small via ONNX; no torch, runs anywhere.
options.note: English-only; lowest measured retrieval.

options.label: Multilingual small CPU model
options.detail: A multilingual ONNX embedder of similar size as the core default.
options.note: Fixes non-English (P-10); needs a quality check against bge-small.

options.label: Hardware-detected profile
options.detail: CPU default B; when a GPU and the [st] extra are present, a 0.6B instruction embedder (Qwen3-Embedding class) with Matryoshka truncation.
options.note: Best quality where hardware allows; two vector spaces to manage.

options.label: Hosted embedder
options.detail: Provider embedding API as default.
options.note: Every stored text leaves the host.

why: QWEN_STACK_RESULTS shows the 0.6B GPU embedder wins at equal time when batched; a CPU multilingual default keeps D-03 slim and supports G-P1. Hardware choice must be pinned per store, since switching needs P-25's re-embed.

title: Reranker model and when to run it
question: Which reranker, if any, should be the default, and should it run on every read or only when it pays?
today: read.rerank off by default (config/schema.py:333); fastembed, flashrank, litellm and qwen3 options; rerank_max_top_k, rerank_gate and rerank_blend exist. Measured: every reranker lowered retrieval sufficiency 1-2 points and cut context 35-50% at +30-35% wall-clock; jina-reranker-v3.5 196 pairs/s vs Qwen3-Reranker-4B 4-bit 35 pairs/s.
others: Hindsight: CPU cross-encoder is the recall bottleneck (length-bucket batching 36-54% faster). Mem0: optional LLM reranker. MemOS: MMR plus relevance gate, no cross-encoder by default. Graphiti: balanced cross-encoder shortlist.

options.label: Off by default (today)
options.detail: No reranker unless configured.
options.note: Measured best sufficiency; larger context.

options.label: Small reranker as context trimmer
options.detail: A fast cross-encoder on GPU (or CPU ONNX) used to cut context under a budget, blended with the retrieval score rather than replacing it.
options.note: 35-50% fewer reader tokens for ~1 point of recall.

options.label: Gated reranker
options.detail: Run only when the retrieval score spread is flat or the candidate pool exceeds the budget.
options.note: Pays only on ambiguous reads; gate thresholds need calibration per store.

options.label: LLM reranker
options.detail: The worker model scores candidates.
options.note: Strong but a model call on the hot path.

why: Measured rerankers cost recall but save reader tokens, so they should run when the token saving matters (hosted reader, tight budget) and the gate says the ranking is uncertain; off stays the default.
owner_note: Standing owner decision (2026-10-11): jina-reranker-v3.5 is the reranker; no further reranker testing. Answer this only for when and where it runs, or confirm.

title: GPU and CPU placement of models
question: How should embedder, reranker, small extractors and the generative model share CPU and GPU on one host?
today: Each component picks its own device: fastembed CPU, st embedder/reranker by embedding.device / read.rerank_device (None = CPU), LLM in Ollama on GPU; nothing coordinates them, and eval arms run two at a time on one 16 GB GPU.
others: LightMem: compression, segmentation and embedding all local GPU. Hindsight: CPU reranker, FP16 on MPS 27-36% faster. MemOS: optional in-process HF/vLLM model.

options.label: Per-component device keys (today)
options.detail: Each model has its own device setting.
options.note: Easy to oversubscribe VRAM and contend with the LLM.

options.label: Encoders on CPU, LLM owns GPU
options.detail: Embedders and rerankers default to ONNX CPU; GPU reserved for the generative model.
options.note: Predictable; batch embedding 5-10x slower than GPU.

options.label: Device planner
options.detail: One placement step at start: detect devices and VRAM, place models by a priority list, reserve LLM context memory, report the plan in describe().
options.note: Best use of one box; more start-up logic.

options.label: Separate inference service
options.detail: All models behind one local inference server (vLLM/TEI) that schedules the GPU.
options.note: Proper scheduling; another service to run.

why: Measured GPU embedders are 80-90x cheaper per token when batched, but they share VRAM with a 9B reader; an explicit plan avoids out-of-memory and makes speed claims reproducible (RV10).

title: Batching and concurrency of model work
question: How should model work be batched and run concurrently across turns, namespaces and read legs?
today: Embeddings batched (embedding.batch_size 32, config/schema.py:130); one ordered window queue per namespace in an asyncio task (workers/windows.py:433-488); sleep batches 30/50 per call; read legs run sequentially (no gather); reranker batches of 8 in a worker thread.
others: MemOS: dispatcher with 50 workers, 4 extractors in parallel per window. Hindsight: four recall arms in parallel; retain sub-batches processed concurrently. Nemori: LLM concurrency 10, serialised per (agent, user). LightMem: ThreadPoolExecutor max 5.

options.label: Serial per namespace, sequential reads (today)
options.detail: Ordered queue per namespace; legs one after another.
options.note: Order-safe; reads slower than needed.

options.label: Parallel read legs
options.detail: Run independent retrieval legs with gather; writes unchanged.
options.note: Lower read latency; DB connection pressure.

options.label: B plus global LLM semaphore
options.detail: Namespaces processed concurrently, ordered within a namespace, under one configurable model concurrency limit matched to the server's slots.
options.note: Throughput for multi-user; needs per-namespace locks shared with sleep (G-W38).

options.label: C plus cross-namespace micro-batching
options.detail: Coalesce embedding and small-model requests from several namespaces into one batch.
options.note: Best GPU use; tenant mixing in one batch must keep isolation.

why: Multi-user workloads need cross-namespace throughput, while per-namespace order is a correctness property for supersede; a semaphore matches local server slots.

title: Latency budgets and time-to-searchable
question: What latency budgets should v2 state for the hot path and for the time until a turn's derived items are searchable?
today: Write returns after raw deposit with no model call; window call runs after write() returns (2.7 s per 9B call vs 55-210 ms hot path); edges wait for the sleep stage; no stated p95 targets (RV10 asks for a manifest).
others: Mem0: vendor p50 0.88 s, slow-query notice at 2 s. Hindsight: recall 100-600 ms, retain 500-2,000 ms per batch. EverMemOS: background index sub-second, 10-15 s under load. Mnemon: warm search 14-18 ms.

options.label: No stated budgets (today)
options.detail: Measured ad hoc.
options.note: Regressions go unnoticed.

options.label: Hot-path budgets only
options.detail: write p95 <= 250 ms, zero-LLM read p95 <= 300 ms on a reference box; model work never on the hot path.
options.note: Fast API; derived layers may lag unboundedly.

options.label: B plus time-to-searchable SLO
options.detail: Also target raw turn searchable at commit and derived items p95 <= N s at stated load, with queue delay and backlog age exported.
options.note: Freshness visible to callers; needs durable queue telemetry.

options.label: Inline derivation option
options.detail: Allow write to wait for derived items when a caller needs read-your-write on facts.
options.note: Strong consistency at ~13-49x write cost.

why: G-W49's gate already names p95 turn-to-searchable-edge; RV10 requires end-to-end p50/p95 and freshness at matched load. A flush barrier (close_session/flush_windows) covers callers needing D.

title: Cost ledger scope and spend limits
question: What should the cost ledger record, at which granularity, and should it enforce spend limits?
today: model_usage per role (engine.py:13257) and usage per prompt_version (#33); window_stats ~40 counters for call 1 (engine.py:13788); sleep layers lack failure and grounding counters; in-process only, tokens estimated chars/4 when the provider gives none (G-W13 partial).
others: LightMem: per-stage calls and tokens. Nemori: per-phase accounting with a hard token budget. Honcho: per-call token telemetry. MemMachine: per-phase Prometheus latency histograms.

options.label: In-process counters (today)
options.detail: Per role and prompt; reset on restart.
options.note: Good for evals, nothing for operations.

options.label: Uniform per-layer ledger
options.detail: Same counters (calls, input/output tokens, retries, failures, grounded/ungrounded, queue delay) for every derived layer and namespace, exported via OpenTelemetry metrics.
options.note: Comparable costs per layer; metric cardinality per namespace.

options.label: B plus persisted ledger and budgets
options.detail: Ledger rows persisted as events; optional per-namespace and per-layer budgets that defer (not drop) derivation when spent; money estimate from a price table.
options.note: Bounded spend for paid providers; deferral must be durable.

why: G-W13 asks for the same counters on every layer plus an optional write budget; RV20 requires stage and deployment labels on cost claims, which a persisted ledger provides. Budgets off by default.

title: Role of small local extractors
question: Which jobs should go to small local models (GLiNER2, spaCy, encoders) instead of the generative model?
today: GLiNER2 ([ner], D-28) for entity extraction and the decision planner (ADR-052: rules first, then plain-label GLiNER2 options, held-out 0.939 vs 0.388); spaCy rejected for core (D-28); topic boundaries from embeddings (core/window.py:108-173).
others: Graphiti: optional gliner2 extra for local NER. LightMem: LLMLingua-2 BERT for compression and topic segmentation. Mem0: spaCy for entity hints. Mnemon: cheap System-1 LLM instead of encoders.

options.label: Entities and routing only (today)
options.detail: GLiNER2 for NER and planner labels; LLM for facts.
options.note: Narrow use of a cheap model.

options.label: Small-model pre-pass for every window
options.detail: GLiNER2 extracts entities, dates, sensitivity and an importance label before the LLM call; the LLM receives them as hints and skips windows with nothing extractable.
options.note: Fewer and shorter LLM calls; hint errors can bias extraction.

options.label: Small-model-only write tier
options.detail: Without a bound LLM, entities, relations and typed spans come from GLiNER2 alone.
options.note: Model-free graph; weak on facts and time.

options.label: spaCy pipeline
options.detail: spaCy NER/dependency parse as the default local layer.
options.note: Mature but per-language models; rejected for core by D-28.

why: ADR-052 shows rules plus GLiNER2 beat the model alone on a held-out set; a pre-pass that gates empty windows and supplies name hints reduces calls (P-14). C is the degraded mode for P-03.

title: Activation (KV-cache) memory
question: Should v2 keep memory as KV-cache activations (prefilled working memory reused across turns), and at what scope?
today: Not present (BD-7 by design): reader runs in Ollama; KV reuse needs an in-process model; llama.cpp adapter exists with n_ctx 8192 (services/llm/llama_cpp.py:27) but no prefix persistence.
others: MemOS: prefills WorkingMemory into a HuggingFace or vLLM KV cache and reuses it. Mnemon: republishes an unchanged View to keep the provider cache warm. Hindsight: provider prompt caching only.

options.label: No KV memory (today)
options.detail: Rebuild context per turn; rely on server prefix caching only.
options.note: Simple; repeated prefill of stable blocks.

options.label: Stable-block prefix reuse
options.detail: Order stable context (profile card, standing answers) first and keep it identical across turns so server prefix caches hit.
options.note: Most of the gain with no KV handling; needs P-08.

options.label: Persisted KV per user
options.detail: In-process llama.cpp or vLLM saves KV state for a user's working block and restores it.
options.note: Model- and version-locked activations; erasure must purge them.

why: Prefill is ~10% of local call time (G-W45), so persisted KV buys little now and adds a model-locked store that forget must reach (RV21); revisit with the in-process adapter.

title: Model upgrades and re-derivation
question: When the embedder, extractor model or a write prompt changes, what should happen to vectors and derived records made by the old one?
today: Embedder change without rebuild is detected only as a dimension mismatch error (engine.py:1051); Engine.rebuild() replays projectors from the log (engine.py:13357); derived records carry prompt_version but there is no selective re-derivation by model or prompt.
others: Graphiti (Combined): periodic full rebuild of profiles from raw history to stop drift. memU: unchanged segments not re-embedded. Cognee: incremental loading skips processed items. Mem0: no re-derivation path.

options.label: Manual rebuild (today)
options.detail: Operator runs rebuild; mismatches raise.
options.note: Same-dimension embedder swaps go undetected and mix vector spaces.

options.label: Versioned vector spaces
options.detail: Each vector carries embedder id; a new embedder builds a shadow index in the background and switches atomically when complete.
options.note: No mixed spaces or downtime; double storage during migration.

options.label: B plus selective re-derivation
options.detail: Derived records whose derivation fingerprint (P-12) is stale are queued for lazy or scheduled re-derivation from raw turns, oldest-used last; old versions kept until replaced.
options.note: Memory improves with models; re-derivation cost needs the budget in P-22.

options.label: Freeze derived, new data only
options.detail: Old records stay as they were; only new turns use the new model.
options.note: Cheap; quality and format drift across the store.

why: Raw turns are durable in the event log, so re-derivation is possible; the fingerprint from P-12 targets only stale records, and RV07's generation checks stop stale results being published after forget.

title: Adoption gate for any behaviour change
question: What must a change pass before it may become a default in v2?
today: Two separate scripts: evals/eval_focus.py scores against the slice's stored labels and treats --ref as informational (eval_focus.py:100,109), so a reference run itself printed PROMOTE on 2026-10-11; evals/eval_blind.py:15,59 confirms on the questions two runs share and can confirm with one blind set missing; GAP_TO_SOLUTION_PLAN.md section 3 rules 3-7 are written policy, not code.
others: Mnemon: per-run commit, data checksums and collect.py that recomputes results byte for byte, but developed on the reported sets. LightMem: baselines rerun in the same harness with per-stage accounting, single run. Mem0, Honcho, EverMemOS: single vendor runs with lenient judges and no adoption rule at all.

options.label: Keep today's two scripts
options.detail: Focus-slice verdict from stored labels, blind check on the intersecting questions, written rules enforced by hand.
options.note: Cheap, but adopted a known-null run on 2026-10-11 and can confirm on one dataset.

options.label: Single paired gate in code
options.detail: One gate tool: paired per-item comparison against a named reference with matching manifest, every in-scope dev set present, per-dataset cluster uncertainty, per-slice non-inferiority; refuses to print a verdict when anything is missing.
options.note: Turns written rules 3-6 into an executable refusal; moderate build effort.

options.label: B plus one frozen blind run
options.detail: As B, then the frozen configuration runs once on the sealed blind sets with a pre-registered metric and tolerance; the blind result is never used for tuning and a missing set means no confirmation.
options.note: Costs one extra GPU unit per adoption; removes development-pool overfitting from claims.

options.label: C plus repeated null controls
options.detail: As C, and the gate is periodically run on known-null changes (seed swap, identical rerun) to estimate the false adoption rate; the margin is widened if nulls pass more often than declared.
options.note: Measures the gate itself; doubles some GPU spend.

why: G-E1 and RV12: eval_focus printed PROMOTE for the reference and for a net -1 change on 2026-10-11, and eval_blind can confirm with a set missing. C closes both defects; D's null controls can run as an occasional audit rather than per adoption (RV12 warns no gate can promise a seed swap never passes).

title: Role of each benchmark in v2
question: Which datasets are development pools, which are blind gates, and which are only descriptive in v2?
today: Development: LoCoMo cat 1-5 (dev/held-out split by conversation) and OP-Bench (dev 331 / held-out 528, I27).
